descriptors.title: Early human migration
descriptors.description: theories and historical interpretations about early human evolution and migration, such as the theory that people moved out of Africa and the causes of migration to other parts of the world, including Australia
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe significant individuals, events and ideas in Australia's post-Federation history and explain how migration to Australia changed society (AC9HS6K01, AC9HS6K03). They have not yet studied human prehistory, early human evolution, or the movement of peoples before written records. They have not worked with geological or archaeological timescales, or with theories about human origins.
elaborations: identifying different theories regarding human evolution such as the Out of Africa Theory and the Modern Theory of Evolution
describing how environmental changes, such as climate change and desertification, triggered the movement of peoples from Africa
identifying how different approaches, such as the use of excavation and stratigraphy, oral history and the data derived from radiocarbon dating, inform historical interpretations

nodes.label: Theories of human evolution
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify competing theories about early human evolution, including the Out of Africa Theory and the Modern Theory of Evolution, and describe what each theory proposes about human origins.
criteria: Names and briefly describes the Out of Africa Theory as the predominant theory of early human origins.
Identifies that historians and scientists work with competing or evolving theories rather than a single settled account of human evolution.
Uses the term 'theory' correctly in a historical/scientific context — as an evidence-based interpretation, not a guess.

width.minimum: Identify and briefly describe the Out of Africa Theory as the major theory of human evolution — that anatomically modern humans evolved in Africa and spread outward.
width.typical: Identify and describe both the Out of Africa Theory and the Modern Theory of Evolution, noting what distinguishes them and why historians and scientists work with competing interpretations of human origins.
wider: Explore how the Out of Africa Theory has been refined over time as new genetic and archaeological evidence has emerged, including debates about whether there was a single dispersal or multiple waves.
Compare how different knowledge systems — scientific, archaeological, and First Nations oral traditions — offer different but potentially complementary accounts of human origins.
Investigate how the concept of 'theory' in historical and scientific inquiry differs from everyday usage, connecting to how historians use evidence to build and revise interpretations.

modes.reason: Students at Year 7 entry have no prior schema for deep-time human history. They need to accumulate a basic repertoire of what these theories propose before they can reason about causes of migration or evaluate evidence. This node builds the conceptual vocabulary (evolution, migration, dispersal, interpretation) that underpins all subsequent nodes.

The comparison between scientific and First Nations knowledge systems about human origins is inherently rich — it surfaces questions about how we know what we know about the deep past, and raises issues of cultural authority and epistemic pluralism. Advancing students benefit from encountering multiple knowledge systems as complementary rather than competing, building the understanding that different epistemological approaches coexist.

nodes.label: Environmental causes of migration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how environmental changes — including climate change and desertification — triggered the movement of early humans out of Africa and into other parts of the world.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot connect environmental change to migration as a causal mechanism will treat K02's arrival causes as disconnected facts rather than an extension of the same causal chain — the push-pull logic that explains departure from Africa is the same logic that explains arrival in Sahul.
criteria: Describes at least one specific environmental change (e.g. desertification, climate shift) and explains how it created conditions that triggered migration.
Identifies that environmental change caused early humans to move in search of resources — not simply that they 'chose' to migrate.
Places early human migration out of Africa in a plausible chronological context (hundreds of thousands of years ago).

width.minimum: Describe at least one major environmental trigger (e.g. climate change, desertification) that caused early humans to migrate out of Africa.
width.typical: Describe how a range of environmental changes — climate change, desertification, and shifting resource availability — combined to push and pull early human populations across different regions, including movement toward and eventually into Australia.
wider: Examine specific geographical routes proposed for early human migration out of Africa (e.g. the coastal route, the northern route through the Levant), and how environmental conditions shaped which routes were viable.

Investigate how the concept of 'push and pull factors' used in modern migration studies applies to early human migration — connecting deep-time history to contemporary geographic and historical frameworks.
Explore how rising and falling sea levels during glacial periods created and closed land bridges, affecting where early humans could and could not travel.

modes.reason: The causal chain from environmental change → resource pressure → population movement is not self-evident to Year 7 students. They need the reasoning scaffold made explicit: what changed in the environment, how that affected survival, and why movement was a response. Without this scaffold, students list environmental changes without connecting them to migration as a human response.

nodes.label: Evidence types and interpretations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different types of evidence used by historians and archaeologists — including excavation and stratigraphy, oral history, and radiocarbon dating — and describe how each type informs interpretations about early human migration.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate evidence with proof will apply a naive reliability model in all subsequent source analysis (S03–S04), treating a single source as settling interpretive claims rather than understanding that interpretations are built from converging lines of evidence.
criteria: Names at least two distinct evidence types and describes what each can reveal about early human migration.
Explains that interpretations about early human migration are based on multiple types of evidence, not a single source.
Does not treat evidence as synonymous with proof — recognises that evidence informs and supports interpretations while leaving room for revision.

width.minimum: Identify at least two types of evidence (e.g. stratigraphy, radiocarbon dating) and describe in basic terms what each can tell us about early human migration.
width.typical: Identify and describe three evidence types — excavation and stratigraphy, oral history, and radiocarbon dating — explaining what each reveals about early human migration and why using multiple evidence types produces stronger interpretations.
wider: Examine how genetic evidence (e.g. DNA analysis of ancient remains, mitochondrial DNA tracing) has been used alongside archaeological evidence to map migration routes, including the movement of peoples to Australia.

Explore the limitations of each evidence type — what stratigraphy cannot tell us, where radiocarbon dating has error ranges, and how oral histories can preserve long-timescale knowledge — and why historians must triangulate across sources.
Investigate specific examples where different evidence types have produced conflicting interpretations of the same migration event, and how historians have responded to that conflict.

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate 'evidence' with 'proof', treating a single piece of evidence as settling an interpretation. Exposure to multiple, distinct evidence types — each with different strengths and limitations — helps students see that interpretations are built from converging lines of evidence, not confirmed by a single source. Broader contexts (stratigraphy, oral history, radiocarbon dating, DNA) are specifically what resolves this misconception.

The logic of how evidence informs interpretation — rather than proves it — requires explicit scaffolding. Students need to understand the inference chain: evidence type → what it can detect → what interpretive claim it supports → what it cannot resolve. This reasoning structure is foundational for all subsequent source-analysis skills in the S strand.

descriptors.title: Arrival on the Australian continent
descriptors.description: theories about the causes and effects of the arrival of early First Nations Australians on the Australian continent and their migration routes across the continent
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify competing theories of early human evolution and migration, describe how environmental changes drove movement out of Africa, and identify how different evidence types inform interpretations (AC9HH7K01). They have not yet studied the specific causes, routes, or effects of the arrival of early peoples on the Australian continent.
elaborations: investigating how scientific techniques have been used to establish the arrival of humans to the mega-continent known as Sahul; for example, use of radiocarbon (C14) and Thermoluminescence (TL) dating techniques used to date archaeological sites related to early human occupation such as Lake Mungo, and genetic research to map the movement of people
investigating how the ancestors of the early First Peoples of Australia were seafarers and examining the likely effects this had on the movement of people to the continent

examining online maps and information to investigate the relationship between geographical features and the location of known ancient sites on the mega-continent known as Sahul; for example, investigating the vegetation types and water sources in different parts of the continent and how they reflect the location of ancient sites

investigating the techniques used to predict the chronology and the routes taken in the dispersal of early First Nations Australians across the continent; for example, using online information that explains how research into ancient landscapes, waterways, terrain and important early First Nations Australians' habitation sites can model the movement of people across the continent, or how DNA taken from hair samples can track the genetic connections of First Nations Australians back to specific parts of Australia as far back as tens of thousands of years ago

nodes.label: Seafaring and arrival — causes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the causes of early First Nations Australians' arrival on the continent, including that their ancestors were seafarers who crossed water to reach Sahul, and identify the geographical context of that crossing.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reason from sea-level context → land configuration of Sahul/Sunda → remaining water gap → deliberate water crossing lack the geographic foundation for N2's route evidence and N3's effects discussion — both depend on understanding the physical reality of the arrival.
criteria: Identifies that early First Nations Australians' ancestors were seafarers who crossed a water gap to reach Sahul.
Names Sahul as the mega-continent including present-day Australia and describes its geographical extent during periods of lower sea level.
Describes the arrival as deliberate and skilled, not accidental drift.

width.minimum: Describe that the ancestors of early First Nations Australians were seafarers who crossed a water gap to reach the mega-continent known as Sahul, and that this was a deliberate and skilled migration.
width.typical: Describe the geographical context of the arrival — the mega-continent Sahul, the water gaps between island-hopping points, and the seafaring capability required — and explain why this migration is significant as one of the earliest long-distance ocean crossings in human history.
wider: Investigate the estimated timeframe of arrival (at least 65,000 years ago) and examine what evidence — radiocarbon dating, TL dating, genetic research — underpins these estimates.

Explore the geographical relationship between Sunda (Southeast Asia landmass during lower sea levels) and Sahul, and how changing sea levels during glacial periods affected the size and location of the water gap.
Examine how the concept of 'seafaring' challenges older assumptions about early human capability, and why this discovery changed historical and archaeological interpretations of early migration.

modes.reason: Students often assume early migration was overland or accidental. The reasoning chain — sea levels during glacial period → land configuration of Sahul/Sunda → remaining water gap → deliberate boat crossing — needs to be made explicit, otherwise students cannot connect the geographical evidence to the seafaring conclusion.

nodes.label: Migration routes across the continent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe likely migration routes taken by early First Nations Australians across the continent, and identify the types of evidence — ancient sites, geographical features, genetic research — used to map those routes.
criteria: Describes at least one type of evidence used to map migration routes across the continent.
Explains that multiple migration routes are proposed, reflecting the limits of available evidence rather than historical confusion.
Identifies at least one specific ancient site or geographical feature in the context of dispersal across the continent.

width.minimum: Describe at least one proposed migration route across the continent and identify one type of evidence used to support it (e.g. ancient habitation sites, DNA research).
width.typical: Describe how researchers use ancient habitation sites, geographical features (waterways, terrain), and genetic research (including DNA from hair samples) to model how early First Nations Australians dispersed across the continent, and explain why multiple routes are proposed rather than a single path.
wider: Examine specific ancient sites — such as Lake Mungo (Willandra Lakes), Madjedbebe, and others — and what their location and dating reveal about the chronology and routes of dispersal.
Investigate how DNA research has been used to track genetic connections of First Nations Australians to specific parts of Australia, and what this reveals about population dispersal.
Explore how ancient landscape features — including now-submerged coastlines, ancient river systems, and vegetation corridors — shaped where people could travel and settle.

modes.reason: Students commonly expect a single, definitive migration route — a misconception that multiple evidence types and the probabilistic nature of ancient site distribution can resolve. Examining different site locations, different evidence methods, and why researchers propose multiple dispersal routes rather than one helps students see that historical interpretation of deep-time events is inherently multi-stranded.

nodes.label: Effects of arrival
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the effects of early First Nations Australians' arrival on the continent, including the establishment of cultures across diverse environments and the beginnings of the world's oldest continuing civilisations.
criteria: Describes at least one concrete effect of early First Nations Australians' arrival and dispersal across the continent.
Connects the diversity of environments across the continent to the development of culturally diverse societies.
Does not treat the arrival as a single event at a single location — recognises it as an extended process of dispersal across a large continent.

width.minimum: Describe at least one effect of the arrival of early First Nations Australians on the continent — for example, the establishment of diverse cultures adapted to different environments across Sahul/Australia.
width.typical: Describe multiple effects of the arrival and dispersal of early First Nations Australians: the development of culturally and environmentally diverse societies across the continent, the beginnings of cultural practices that have continued for tens of thousands of years, and the relationship between geographical dispersal and cultural diversity.
wider: Examine how early First Nations Australians' dispersal into diverse environments — coastal, desert, tropical, temperate — led to the development of distinct languages, technologies, and cultural practices adapted to each environment.
Investigate how the arrival and dispersal of early peoples may have intersected with the megafauna extinction debate — examining the evidence and the competing interpretations.

Explore how the effects of early arrival are still visible in contemporary First Nations cultures — in language diversity, in kinship systems, and in the oral traditions that preserve knowledge of ancient events.

modes.reason: This node integrates the causes of arrival (seafaring, environmental context from K01–K02) with what that arrival produced. Students must coordinate the geographical, temporal, and cultural dimensions of the arrival story — connecting where people came from, how they got here, where they dispersed, and what they built — to reach the descriptor's full demand.

descriptors.title: Continuity over deep time
descriptors.description: how First Nations Australians are the world's oldest continuing cultures, displaying evidence of both continuity and change over deep time
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the arrival of early First Nations Australians on the continent, identify evidence for migration routes, and describe effects of that arrival including the establishment of diverse cultures (AC9HH7K02). They have not yet examined the evidence for cultural continuity over deep time, nor the concept of 'deep time' as a historical framework.
elaborations: investigating dating methods used by archaeologists for the study of early First Nations Australians; for example, the use of the 'Before Present' (BP) dating system

exploring how we know about continuities and changes in First Nations Australians' cultures; for example, the archaeological research showing evidence of occupation and the lives of First Nations Australians during the Pleistocene epoch at sites such as Lake Mungo and Kutikina Cave

exploring evidence of continuities and changes in the ancient period at specific sites; for example, dating the creation of pictographs and the carving of petroglyphs at sites such as the Dampier Archipelago, Grampians National Park, Kakadu National Park, Koonalda Cave, Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park, Preminghana, and the West Kimberley
exploring evidence of continuing culture that was evident in the ancient period, such as the use of ochre

examining First Nations Australians' views on creation and changes in the landscape that have been passed down through oral tradition, such as the existence of megafauna, changes from wetter to drier climates and changes in vegetation in central Australia

nodes.label: Deep time as a historical concept
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what 'deep time' means in a historical context, describe the Before Present (BP) dating system, and place First Nations Australians' cultural history on a deep-time scale.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot correctly use BP dating and place events on a deep-time scale cannot anchor continuity or change evidence in N2 and N3 chronologically — claims about what persisted or changed across 65,000 years become unanchored without the convention to express and compare those timescales.
criteria: Explains what 'deep time' means as a historical concept and why it requires different chronological frameworks.
Describes the BP (Before Present) dating system and can correctly interpret a BP date (e.g. 30,000 BP = 30,000 years before 1950).
Correctly places First Nations Australians' cultural history in a deep-time context, using a scale that conveys the meaning of 65,000+ years.

width.minimum: Explain that 'deep time' refers to the vast timescales of human prehistory (tens of thousands of years) and describe the BP (Before Present) dating system as the convention used by archaeologists for deep-time events.
width.typical: Explain the concept of deep time and why it requires different chronological conventions (BP vs BCE/CE), describe how the BP system works, and place First Nations Australians' cultural continuity in context as a history spanning at least 65,000 years — longer than any other documented cultural continuity on Earth.
wider: Compare the deep-time timeline of First Nations Australians' cultural continuity with other ancient civilisations (e.g. ancient Egypt at ~5,000 years, Mesopotamia at ~6,000 years) to establish the significance of 65,000+ years of continuous culture.
Explore how the Pleistocene and Holocene epochs used by geologists and archaeologists map onto First Nations Australians' cultural history, and how geological time and cultural time intersect.
Investigate the dating conventions used across different disciplines — BP for archaeology, BCE/CE for written history — and discuss why different conventions serve different purposes.

modes.reason: Chronological reasoning across orders of magnitude (65,000 years vs 200 years vs 6,000 years) is a precision skill that students commonly mishandle. The BP system, its relationship to BCE/CE, and the capacity to place events on a deep-time scale all require fluency through practice. This is a procedural-conceptual threshold before students can engage meaningfully with evidence of continuity and change.

nodes.label: Evidence of continuity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe specific archaeological and cultural evidence that demonstrates the continuity of First Nations Australians' cultures over deep time, including evidence from key sites.
criteria: Identifies at least two specific pieces of evidence from different sites or evidence types that demonstrate cultural continuity over deep time.
Explains what each piece of evidence demonstrates about continuity — not just lists evidence but connects it to the claim.
Uses at least one specific site name and places it geographically and chronologically.

width.minimum: Describe at least one specific piece of evidence — from an archaeological site or cultural practice — that demonstrates the continuity of First Nations Australians' cultures over deep time (e.g. ochre use, rock art at Kakadu, occupation at Lake Mungo).
width.typical: Describe multiple forms of evidence for cultural continuity — archaeological evidence from sites such as Lake Mungo, Kutikina Cave, and rock art sites (Dampier Archipelago, Kakadu, Grampians, Uluru-Kata Tjuta), and cultural continuity such as ongoing use of ochre — explaining what each piece of evidence demonstrates about continuity.
wider: Investigate specific rock art sites in detail — such as the Bradshaw/Gwion Gwion paintings, petroglyphs at the Dampier Archipelago, or ochre paintings at Koonalda Cave — examining the dating methods used and what the art reveals about cultural continuity.

Explore how oral traditions have preserved knowledge of environmental events (megafauna, sea-level changes) over tens of thousands of years, and what this reveals about the cultural mechanisms of continuity.

Examine the archaeological evidence at Lake Mungo and Kutikina Cave in detail — what was found, how it was dated, and what it tells us about daily life, cultural practice, and continuity across the Pleistocene epoch.

modes.reason: Students commonly treat continuity as an abstract claim rather than something demonstrated by specific, varied evidence. Exposure to multiple evidence types and sites — rock art, ochre use, artefacts, oral traditions — each showing continuity in different ways, helps students build a genuine understanding that cultural continuity is evidenced, not merely asserted. Single-site focus risks students treating continuity as a local rather than continent-wide phenomenon.

nodes.label: Evidence of change over deep time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe evidence of change in First Nations Australians' cultures over deep time, and explain that the concept of 'oldest continuing culture' encompasses both continuity and change — not a static or unchanging society.
criteria: Describes at least one specific example of change in First Nations Australians' cultures over deep time with reference to evidence.
Explains that continuity and change coexist — 'oldest continuing culture' does not mean unchanging or static.
Does not treat change as evidence against continuity — correctly understands continuity as cultural persistence, not cultural stasis.

width.minimum: Describe at least one example of change in First Nations Australians' cultures over deep time (e.g. changes in technology, responses to environmental change, shifts in cultural practice).
width.typical: Describe multiple examples of change across deep time — environmental responses, technological development, shifts in settlement patterns — and explain how these changes coexist with cultural continuity, challenging the misconception that 'oldest continuing culture' means 'unchanging culture'.
wider: Examine specific documented changes: the development and refinement of stone tool technologies, changes in population distribution in response to aridification, and adaptations to rising sea levels — connecting each change to its environmental or social context.

Explore how First Nations Australians' oral traditions capture and transmit knowledge of change — such as stories of sea-level rise, the existence of megafauna, and changes in landscape — as evidence that change was recognised, documented, and culturally processed.

Investigate how change within continuity is a distinctive feature of First Nations Australians' cultures compared to ancient civilisations that were disrupted, conquered, or ended — and what this comparison reveals about resilience and adaptation.

modes.reason: A persistent misconception is that 'oldest continuing culture' implies a culture frozen in time. Multiple examples of change — technological, environmental, social — across different periods and regions specifically dislodges this. Breadth of examples (different types of change, different periods, different regions) is what resolves the misconception, not deeper analysis of a single change.

This node integrates the continuity evidence (Node 2) with change evidence into the descriptor's full demand — that First Nations Australians' cultures display evidence of BOTH continuity and change. Students must hold both together: same cultures persisting, adapting, innovating across 65,000+ years.

descriptors.title: Environmental response over time
descriptors.description: how First Nations Australians have responded to environmental processes and changes over time
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain that First Nations Australians' cultures display both continuity and change over deep time, and describe evidence of cultural adaptation including responses to environmental change (AC9HH7K03). They have not yet examined specific environmental processes in detail — rising sea levels, aridification, megafauna — or how particular communities responded to each.
elaborations: explaining the effects of environmental changes on First Nations Australians across Australia, such as rising sea levels (for example, the loss of the land bridge to Tasmania and the formation of the Torres Strait Islands from an existing land bridge) and the aridification of some landscapes, such as Lake Mungo

investigating how accounts of rising sea levels that occurred between 18,000 and 7,000 years ago have been passed down through the oral traditions of First Nations Australians; for example, stories in the Boonwurrung (Port Phillip) Country about the loss of kangaroo hunting grounds, and those in the Nukunu (Spencer Gulf) Country about the sea swallowing up the land

investigating the megafauna that inhabited Australia in the Pleistocene epoch and discussing how it may have impacted on the sustainable harvesting of game by First Nations Australians, both prior to and after the extinction of megafauna

exploring evidence of how First Nations Australians responded to environmental changes in the Holocene epoch; for example, archaeological evidence that people maintained seasonal presence in the Willandra Lakes region at times when water was available, the maritime specialisation of those on the Torres Strait Islands and Cape York around 2,500 BP, and the de-population of islands such as Rottnest, Kangaroo and Flinders islands when cut off from the mainland
investigating the water management techniques used by early First Nations Australians in environments with scarce supplies of fresh water, such as islands and deserts

nodes.label: Environmental changes — sea level and aridification
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the major environmental changes that affected the Australian continent over deep time — including rising sea levels between 18,000 and 7,000 years ago and the aridification of landscapes such as the Willandra Lakes region — and explain their geographical effects.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot connect geological-scale environmental changes to their geographic and human consequences lack the analytical foundation for N3's adaptive responses — they will list adaptive strategies without grounding them in the specific challenges those strategies were responding to.
criteria: Describes at least two specific environmental changes that affected the continent over deep time (e.g. rising sea levels, aridification).
Identifies at least one concrete geographical consequence of each change (e.g. loss of land bridge to Tasmania, drying of Lake Mungo).
Places these changes in a broad chronological context (Pleistocene/Holocene, or thousands to tens of thousands of years ago).

width.minimum: Describe rising sea levels as a major environmental change that affected the continent, including at least one specific geographical effect (e.g. loss of the land bridge to Tasmania, formation of the Torres Strait Islands).
width.typical: Describe both rising sea levels and aridification as significant environmental processes, explaining specific geographical consequences: the loss of the land bridge to Tasmania, the formation of the Torres Strait Islands, the drying of Lake Mungo and the Willandra Lakes region, and how these changes reshaped the continent's geography and ecology.
wider: Map the changes to the coastline and land area of Australia between the Last Glacial Maximum (~20,000 BP) and the present, examining what land was lost and how that affected settlement.
Explore the estimated scale of sea-level rise (over 120 metres since the Last Glacial Maximum) and what that means for the coastlines and communities that existed in now-submerged areas.
Investigate the Holocene epoch as a period of dramatic environmental change following the Pleistocene, and how the transition shaped the continent that contemporary Australians inhabit.

modes.reason: Students struggle to connect geological-scale environmental change to its human consequences. The reasoning chain — sea levels rose → land bridges submerged → communities separated or displaced — requires explicit scaffolding. Without it, students list environmental changes without understanding how they produced specific social and demographic effects.

nodes.label: Oral traditions as evidence of environmental response
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how First Nations Australians' oral traditions have preserved accounts of environmental changes — including sea-level rise — over thousands of years, and explain what this demonstrates about cultural mechanisms for transmitting knowledge.
criteria: Describes at least one specific oral tradition that preserves knowledge of an environmental change, naming the community and the event.
Explains that these oral traditions constitute evidence of both the environmental event and of cultural memory operating over deep time.
Does not dismiss oral tradition as 'just stories' — treats it as a legitimate, evidenced form of historical knowledge.

width.minimum: Describe that First Nations Australians' oral traditions contain accounts of environmental changes such as rising sea levels, and identify at least one example (e.g. Boonwurrung stories of Port Phillip, Nukunu stories of Spencer Gulf).
width.typical: Describe multiple examples of oral traditions preserving accounts of sea-level rise and landscape change — including the Boonwurrung stories of kangaroo hunting grounds lost under Port Phillip, and the Nukunu stories of the sea swallowing the land at Spencer Gulf — and explain how these traditions demonstrate cultural memory operating over thousands of years.
wider: Explore the research methodology used to correlate oral tradition accounts with geological evidence of sea-level change, and examine what this correlation suggests about the reliability and longevity of oral transmission.

Investigate the oral traditions that describe megafauna — such as descriptions of giant animals that match known Pleistocene species — and discuss what this reveals about the timeframes over which oral knowledge can persist.

Examine how oral traditions function as a historical source — comparing what they can and cannot tell us relative to archaeological evidence, and why historians increasingly treat them as serious evidence about deep-time events.

modes.reason: Students commonly undervalue oral tradition as historical evidence, treating written sources and physical artefacts as more 'real'. Exposure to multiple, geographically distinct oral tradition examples — each corroborated by geological evidence — specifically resolves this bias. Breadth across different traditions and different environmental events is what builds the understanding that oral tradition is a legitimate and sophisticated knowledge system.

nodes.label: Adaptive responses — water management and resource strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe specific strategies developed by First Nations Australians in response to environmental challenges, including water management techniques in resource-scarce environments, and explain how these strategies demonstrate sophisticated environmental knowledge.
criteria: Describes at least one specific adaptive strategy and connects it to a specific environmental challenge.
Explains the strategy as evidence of sophisticated environmental knowledge — not just survival instinct.
Does not treat adaptive responses as generic or uniform — recognises that different environments produced different strategies.

width.minimum: Describe at least one specific adaptive strategy developed by First Nations Australians in response to environmental change or scarcity (e.g. water management in arid environments, seasonal movement in the Willandra Lakes region, maritime specialisation on Torres Strait Islands).
width.typical: Describe a range of adaptive strategies across different environments — water management techniques for arid and island environments, seasonal presence and mobility strategies in response to water availability (e.g. Willandra Lakes), maritime specialisation on Torres Strait Islands and Cape York — and explain how each strategy reflects sophisticated knowledge of local environmental conditions.
wider: Examine the archaeological evidence for seasonal presence at the Willandra Lakes region — what this evidence looks like, how it has been dated, and what it tells us about the decision-making strategies of communities managing scarce water resources.

Investigate the de-population of islands such as Rottnest, Kangaroo, and Flinders Islands when they were cut off from the mainland by rising sea levels (~10,000 BP), examining what this reveals about how communities responded when adaptation was no longer viable.

Explore water management techniques in desert and semi-arid environments — including the use of soakages, gnamma holes, and knowledge of seasonal water sources — as evidence of environmental knowledge systems that supported survival in landscapes others would consider uninhabitable.

modes.reason: This node integrates the environmental changes (Node 1) and the oral tradition evidence (Node 2) with the adaptive responses — bringing together what changed, how it was remembered, and what people did about it. Students must coordinate all three dimensions to reach the descriptor's claim: that First Nations Australians responded to environmental processes with sophisticated, evidence-based adaptation.

descriptors.title: Early technological achievements
descriptors.description: the technological achievements of early First Nations Australians, and how these developed in different places and contributed to daily life, and land and water source management
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe how First Nations Australians responded to environmental processes and changes over time, including specific adaptive strategies involving water management and seasonal movement (AC9HH7K04). They have not yet examined the technological achievements of early First Nations Australians as a category in their own right, including the development and sophistication of stone tools, food production systems, and land and water management technologies.
elaborations: investigating chronologies of technological achievements for continuity and change over time, including the development of stone tools and stone-knapping techniques such as ground-edge tools, hafted axes and mill stones

exploring how food production or procurement such as agriculture, aquaculture, nomadism and hunter-gatherer/forager societies were influenced by the environment; for example, people in the Torres Strait Islands and Cape York developing maritime technologies and people in arid environments developing a nomadic lifestyle, and the development of sustainable harvesting practices such as those of the Mithaka People in Queensland's Channel Country

exploring land and water management practices developed by early First Nations Australians, such as cultural burning practices, and the conservation and use of water through the development of weirs, irrigation and water evaporation reduction systems

exploring aquaculture practices developed by early First Nations Australians, such as eel traps of the Gundtitjmara People at Budj Bim, Victoria, the mollusc harvesting of the Kombumerri People on the Gold Coast, Queensland, and stone fish traps used by the Ngemba People at Brewarrina, New South Wales

nodes.label: Stone tool technologies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the development of stone tool technologies by early First Nations Australians — including ground-edge tools, hafted axes, and millstones — and explain what these technologies reveal about cultural and technological sophistication over time.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who lack a concrete repertoire of specific stone tool technologies cannot engage meaningfully with N3's integration task — the descriptor's claim about technological contribution to daily life requires specific examples as raw material for the synthesis.
criteria: Names and describes at least two stone tool technologies and their primary uses.
Explains stone-knapping as a skilled craft requiring specialist knowledge, not simply 'chipping rocks'.
Identifies that tool technologies developed and were refined over time — they were not static.

width.minimum: Describe at least two stone tool technologies (e.g. ground-edge tools, hafted axes, millstones) and explain what each was used for.
width.typical: Describe the development and refinement of stone tool technologies over time — including the shift from core tools to more refined technologies such as ground-edge tools, hafted axes, and millstones — and explain how stone-knapping as a skill represents a body of knowledge transmitted and refined across generations.
wider: Investigate the chronology of stone tool development — from early core and flake tools to the microliths and backed artefacts of later periods — examining what the changes reveal about cognitive and cultural development.

Examine specific stone-knapping techniques and the knowledge required to produce particular tool types, including how regional variation in tool technology reflects both available materials and local needs.
Explore how stone tool technologies have been dated and what they tell us about the distribution of populations and cultural exchange networks across the continent.

modes.reason: Students need a repertoire of specific technology examples before they can reason about development across places or contribution to daily life. Without knowing what ground-edge tools, hafted axes, and millstones actually are and do, the broader claims about technological achievement are abstractions. Building a concrete inventory of technologies is the prerequisite for the integration work in later nodes.

nodes.label: Food production and procurement systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how food production and procurement systems — including agriculture, aquaculture, nomadism, and hunter-gatherer/forager practices — were developed by early First Nations Australians in response to different environments.
criteria: Describes at least two distinct food production or procurement systems and connects each to a specific environmental context.
Explains that different environments produced different food systems — not a single, uniform approach across the continent.
Identifies that these systems reflect sophisticated ecological knowledge, not simply opportunistic foraging.

width.minimum: Describe at least two distinct food production or procurement systems and connect each to an environmental context (e.g. maritime technologies in coastal areas, nomadic strategies in arid environments).
width.typical: Describe a range of food production and procurement systems across different environmental contexts — maritime technologies on Torres Strait Islands and Cape York, nomadic lifestyles in arid environments, forager strategies, and sustainable harvesting practices — explaining how each system reflects sophisticated knowledge of local environments and resources.
wider: Investigate the Mithaka People's sustainable harvesting practices in Queensland's Channel Country as a specific case study — examining what these practices involved, how they were organised, and what they reveal about ecological knowledge.

Explore the distinction between hunter-gatherer/forager practices and agriculture, examining whether the binary is adequate for describing First Nations Australians' sophisticated food systems, some of which involved deliberate cultivation and landscape management.

Examine the development of maritime technologies — canoes, fishing implements, tidal fish traps — in coastal and island communities, and how these technologies enabled access to marine resources that extended food security.

modes.reason: Students commonly apply a single, undifferentiated mental model of hunter-gatherer societies to all First Nations Australians — missing the diversity and sophistication of different food systems across different environments. Exposure to multiple, geographically distinct examples (Torres Strait maritime, Channel Country sustainable harvesting, arid-zone nomadism) specifically resolves this generalisation and builds understanding of environmental-technological diversity.

nodes.label: Land and water management technologies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe specific land and water management technologies developed by early First Nations Australians — including cultural burning, aquaculture systems, weirs, and water management infrastructure — and explain how these contributed to daily life and sustainable resource management.
criteria: Describes at least two specific land or water management technologies with reference to named communities or sites.
Explains how each technology contributed to sustainable resource management — not just what it was, but what problem it solved.
Does not treat these technologies as primitive — uses language that reflects the sophistication and scale of the engineering involved.

width.minimum: Describe at least one land or water management technology (e.g. cultural burning, eel traps, stone fish traps, weirs) and explain its purpose and contribution to resource management.
width.typical: Describe multiple land and water management technologies across different environments — cultural burning practices for land management, aquaculture systems including eel traps (Budj Bim), mollusc harvesting (Kombumerri People), stone fish traps (Brewarrina), weirs and irrigation — and explain how each technology demonstrates deliberate, sustained management of the landscape.
wider: Examine the Budj Bim aquaculture system in detail — its age (at least 6,600 years, older than the Egyptian pyramids), its engineering, how it was identified as a world heritage site, and what it reveals about the scale and sophistication of First Nations water management.

Investigate cultural burning practices as a landscape management technology — examining how controlled burns were used to manage vegetation, promote food sources, and maintain ecological diversity, and how this knowledge is being integrated into contemporary land management.

Explore the Brewarrina fish traps (Baiame's Ngunnhu) as among the world's oldest human-made structures — examining the archaeological evidence for their age, how they functioned, and what they reveal about long-term community infrastructure.

modes.reason: This node integrates stone tool technologies (Node 1) and food systems (Node 2) with land and water management into the descriptor's full demand: a picture of early First Nations Australians as sophisticated technological innovators whose achievements contributed to daily life and sustained resource management at landscape scale. Students must connect technology, food systems, and land management as a coherent whole.

descriptors.title: Social organisation and cultural practice
descriptors.description: the social organisation and cultural practices of early First Nations Australians, and their continuity and change over time
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the technological achievements of early First Nations Australians across different environments, including food systems and land management (AC9HH7K05). They have not yet examined the social organisational structures — moieties, totems, kinship — or the cultural practices and their transmission mechanisms as topics in their own right.
elaborations: examining the social organisation systems of First Nations Australians, such as moieties, totems and kinship groups, and how they determine roles and relationships to others, including how they underpin marriage laws, and their development and significance in areas such as Central Australia during increasing desertification

examining how aspects of social organisation and cultural practices of early First Nations Australians are known because they have been passed on through oral traditions and supported by media such as song, dance, music and visual art representations such as rock paintings; for example, narratives or visual representations related to lore, kinship structures, and responsibilities to the land, seas, waterways, sky and universe

investigating important cultural practices of early First Nations Australians and their continuity and change over time; for example, lore, rites of passage, and the antiquity and types of funerary customs and burial practices such as the early example of cremation at the Willandra Lakes in New South Wales, the tombstone openings of the Torres Strait Islands and the log coffins used by the Yolngu Peoples of Arnhem Land

exploring the existence of defined land, sea and sky territories, and the social and political systems that governed early First Nations Australians' societies, such as land tenure systems, delineation and reciprocal access rights, and the trade and bartering of items such as ochre, medicine and trepang

nodes.label: Social organisation — kinship, moieties, and totems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the social organisation systems of early First Nations Australians — including moieties, totems, and kinship groups — and explain how these systems determine roles, relationships, and responsibilities within communities.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students without a schema for kinship, moieties, and totems cannot understand N3's cultural practices as expressions of these social structures — lore, rites of passage, and funerary customs will be described in isolation from the social organisation that produces and sustains them.
criteria: Describes at least two social organisation structures (e.g. moieties, kinship, totems) and explains what each determines about roles or relationships.
Explains that these systems are interconnected — not isolated categories but a coherent social architecture.
Does not treat kinship in purely Western biological terms — recognises it as a broader system of roles and obligations.

width.minimum: Describe at least one social organisation system (kinship, moieties, or totems) and explain what it determines about roles or relationships within a community.
width.typical: Describe moieties, totems, and kinship groups as interconnected social organisation systems, explaining how they together determine roles and relationships — including marriage laws — and how they developed their particular significance in specific contexts such as Central Australia during increasing desertification.
wider: Examine the practical functions of kinship systems in detail — how they organise obligations of care, resource sharing, conflict resolution, and marriage — connecting social structure to everyday life.
Explore how social organisation systems vary across different regions and language groups, reflecting the diversity of First Nations Australians' societies rather than a single uniform structure.
Investigate how social organisation systems underpin land tenure — the connection between kinship group, Country, and the rights and responsibilities that flow from that connection.

modes.reason: Kinship systems, moieties, and totems are conceptually unfamiliar to most Year 7 students who have no prior schema for social organisation systems different from Western family or class structures. The reasoning chain — how moieties divide a community, how totems mark group identity and obligations, how kinship determines who is 'family' in a system very different from biological parenthood — needs to be explicitly scaffolded before students can reason about continuity and change.

nodes.label: Cultural transmission — oral traditions and expressive arts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how cultural knowledge — including lore, kinship structures, responsibilities to Country, and historical events — has been transmitted through oral traditions supported by song, dance, music, and visual art, and explain what this reveals about cultural continuity.
criteria: Describes oral tradition, song, dance, music, and visual art as interconnected mechanisms for cultural transmission — not just entertainment.
Identifies at least two types of knowledge transmitted through these mechanisms.
Explains how cultural transmission through these mechanisms accounts for cultural continuity over deep time.

width.minimum: Describe that oral traditions, supported by media such as song, dance, and visual art, have been the primary mechanism for transmitting cultural knowledge across generations, and give at least one example of knowledge transmitted this way.
width.typical: Describe how oral traditions function as a cultural transmission mechanism — supported by song, dance, music, and visual art — and explain what kinds of knowledge are transmitted: lore, kinship structures, responsibilities to land and seas, historical narratives, and cultural obligations. Explain how this transmission mechanism accounts for cultural continuity over tens of thousands of years.
wider: Examine specific examples of cultural transmission in detail — rock paintings, ceremonial song cycles, Songlines as geographical and narrative maps — exploring how each medium encodes different types of knowledge.
Investigate the concept of Songlines as a cultural transmission technology that encodes geographical, navigational, and historical knowledge in a form that can be transmitted orally and through song.

Explore the relationship between oral tradition as cultural transmission and the written-record assumption in Western historiography — examining what is lost and what is preserved by each approach, and why oral traditions deserve equal standing as historical sources.

modes.reason: Students frequently undervalue oral tradition and expressive arts as knowledge transmission mechanisms, treating them as cultural performance rather than information systems. Exposure to multiple examples — each showing how different media (song, dance, visual art, narrative) encode different types of knowledge — specifically resolves this misconception and builds understanding of oral tradition as a sophisticated, multi-modal knowledge system.

nodes.label: Cultural practices — lore, rites of passage, and funerary customs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe specific cultural practices of early First Nations Australians — including lore, rites of passage, and funerary customs — and explain how these practices have shown both continuity and change over time.
criteria: Describes at least two distinct cultural practices and explains the social function of each.
Uses at least one specific example with archaeological or cultural evidence (e.g. Willandra Lakes cremation, Torres Strait tombstone openings).
Explains that cultural practices show both continuity (practices maintained over thousands of years) and change (regional variation, adaptation over time).

width.minimum: Describe at least one cultural practice (lore, rites of passage, or funerary customs) and explain its social function within the community.
width.typical: Describe multiple cultural practices — lore as the body of law and knowledge governing social and spiritual life, rites of passage marking transitions between life stages, and funerary customs — and explain how these practices reflect social organisation, responsibilities, and cultural values. Note the antiquity of some practices (e.g. early cremation evidence at Willandra Lakes, ~40,000 BP).
wider: Examine the archaeological evidence for early funerary customs at Willandra Lakes — the earliest known evidence of human cremation (~40,000 BP) — and discuss what this reveals about cultural practices, beliefs about death, and the antiquity of ceremonial life.

Investigate specific funerary customs across different communities — tombstone openings of the Torres Strait Islands, log coffins of the Yolngu Peoples — as examples of cultural practices that display both regional variation and continuity over time.

Explore how lore functions as a comprehensive governance system — covering land rights, environmental management, social relations, and spiritual obligations — and why it represents a sophisticated legal and ethical framework.

modes.reason: This node integrates social organisation (Node 1) and cultural transmission (Node 2) with specific cultural practices, completing the descriptor's demand for an account of social organisation AND cultural practices AND their continuity and change. Students must connect how lore, rites of passage, and funerary customs are both expressions of the social organisation structures described in Node 1 and transmitted through the mechanisms described in Node 2.

descriptors.title: Cultural preservation and heritage
descriptors.description: the cultural obligations of First Nations Australians about significant heritage sites, including ancestral remains, material culture and artefacts, and the role of collaboration between First Nations Australians and other individuals and groups to ensure cultural preservation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the social organisation and cultural practices of early First Nations Australians, including funerary customs, and explain how cultural knowledge has been transmitted through oral traditions and expressive arts (AC9HH7K06). They have not yet examined cultural obligations about heritage sites specifically, or the role of collaboration and institutional frameworks in cultural preservation.
elaborations: recognising how the human remains of early First Nations Australians are the ancestors of contemporary First Nations Peoples of Australia and, as such, any unauthorised disturbance is taken as a serious breach of cultural protocol
exploring how the ancestral remains found at Lake Mungo (Willandra Lakes region) illustrate the issues of ownership, cultural protocols, research and repatriation
examining the importance of consultation with multiple stakeholders when conserving culture and heritage sites; for example, the collaboration between the Traditional Owners and researchers
investigating world heritage criteria for the listing of significant sites such as the Budj Bim and Willandra Lakes regions, and cultural landscapes such as Uluru-Kata Tjuta and Kakadu

examining the role of national and state/territory galleries, libraries, archives, museums, historical societies and field-sites in curating, conserving and showcasing First Nations Australians' histories and cultures

nodes.label: Cultural obligations and ancestral remains
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what cultural obligations First Nations Australians hold regarding significant heritage sites and ancestral remains, and describe why the disturbance of ancestral remains is a serious breach of cultural protocol.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who frame heritage obligations in Western property or conservation terms will misread the Lake Mungo case in N2 — they will analyse it as a legal dispute rather than understanding what the cultural protocol stakes actually are, missing the central dynamic of the case.
criteria: Explains that ancestral remains are understood as ancestors of contemporary First Nations Peoples, not simply archaeological material.
Describes why unauthorised disturbance of ancestral remains is a serious breach of cultural protocol — not just a legal infringement.
Does not frame heritage obligations purely in Western conservation terms — recognises the relational and spiritual dimensions.

width.minimum: Explain that First Nations Australians hold cultural obligations to significant heritage sites and ancestral remains, and that any unauthorised disturbance of ancestral remains constitutes a serious breach of cultural protocol.
width.typical: Explain the cultural obligations of First Nations Australians regarding heritage sites, ancestral remains, and material culture — including that ancestral remains are the ancestors of contemporary First Nations Peoples and that cultural protocols govern their treatment. Describe why these obligations are not simply legal requirements but expressions of ongoing cultural, spiritual, and kinship relationships.
wider: Examine specific examples of cultural protocols governing access to heritage sites — who has authority to speak for a site, what consultation processes are required, and how these protocols interact with Australian heritage law.
Investigate the concept of Country in relation to heritage obligations — how the obligation to care for ancestral remains and sites flows from the relationship between people, Country, and ancestors.

Explore the distinction between 'heritage' as understood in Western conservation frameworks and 'living culture' as understood by First Nations Australians — examining why the two frameworks sometimes produce different priorities.

modes.reason: Students often approach heritage through a Western property/conservation framework, missing the relational and spiritual dimensions of First Nations cultural obligations. The reasoning chain — ancestral remains are ancestors, ancestors are part of ongoing kinship and cultural relationships, therefore disturbance ruptures living relationships, not just archaeological records — needs to be made explicit to overcome the misconception that heritage obligations are simply about protecting old things.

nodes.label: Lake Mungo — ownership, repatriation, and collaboration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how the Lake Mungo case illustrates the issues of ownership, cultural protocols, research, and repatriation that arise when ancestral remains are discovered, and explain the collaborative processes involved in resolving these issues.
criteria: Describes what was found at Lake Mungo and why the find is archaeologically and culturally significant.
Identifies the specific issues raised — ownership, cultural protocols, research access, repatriation — and explains why each matters.
Does not frame the case as a simple conflict between science and culture — recognises the collaborative resolution process.

width.minimum: Describe the Lake Mungo case — what was found, why it is significant, and what issues it raised regarding ownership, cultural protocols, and repatriation.
width.typical: Describe the Lake Mungo case in detail — the discovery of Mungo Man and Mungo Lady, their archaeological significance (among the oldest human remains in Australia), the issues of ownership and cultural protocols they raised for the Mutthi Mutthi, Paakantji, and Ngiyampaa Peoples, and the eventual repatriation process. Explain how this case became a landmark in negotiating the relationship between scientific research and First Nations cultural obligations.
wider: Examine the timeline of the Lake Mungo repatriation — the discovery, the period of scientific study, the advocacy by Traditional Owners, and the eventual return — analysing what this timeline reveals about evolving relationships between research institutions and First Nations communities.

Investigate the broader debate about the repatriation of cultural heritage internationally — such as the Elgin Marbles, Benin Bronzes, or First Nations skeletal collections held in overseas museums — and how the Lake Mungo case connects to these global debates.

Explore how Australian law (e.g. NAGPRA equivalents, ATSIHP Act) governs the treatment and repatriation of First Nations ancestral remains, examining how this legal framework has evolved in response to community advocacy.

modes.reason: The Lake Mungo case is specific and significant, but students need broader context — other repatriation cases, other heritage debates — to understand it as an instance of a wider pattern rather than an isolated incident. Breadth across cases helps students see that the tensions between research access and cultural obligations recur across different sites, different communities, and different countries, and that the collaborative resolution model is not automatic but achieved.

nodes.label: Collaboration and institutional roles in preservation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the roles of multiple stakeholders — Traditional Owners, researchers, government bodies, and institutions — in cultural preservation, and describe how collaboration and world heritage frameworks support the protection of significant sites.
criteria: Identifies at least two stakeholder groups and explains the role each plays in cultural preservation.
Describes at least one institutional mechanism (heritage listing, museum/archive role) and explains how it contributes to preservation.
Explains that effective preservation requires collaboration — not sole control by any single stakeholder.

width.minimum: Describe the roles of at least two stakeholders (e.g. Traditional Owners and research institutions, or government bodies and community groups) in cultural preservation, and identify one institutional mechanism (e.g. world heritage listing, national galleries and archives) that supports preservation.
width.typical: Describe the roles of Traditional Owners, researchers, national and state institutions (galleries, libraries, archives, museums, historical societies), and government bodies in cultural preservation. Explain how collaboration between these stakeholders — rather than any single authority — is required for effective preservation. Describe how world heritage listing (e.g. Budj Bim, Willandra Lakes, Uluru-Kata Tjuta, Kakadu) functions as a mechanism for international recognition and protection.
wider: Examine the world heritage criteria in detail — examining which criteria Budj Bim, Willandra Lakes, and Kakadu satisfy, and what this reveals about how international frameworks assess the significance of First Nations cultural landscapes.

Investigate the roles and responsibilities of specific institutions — such as the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies (AIATSIS) — in curating, repatriating, and making accessible First Nations cultural heritage.

Explore the tensions that can arise in collaborative heritage management — when Traditional Owner priorities, research interests, and tourism/access demands conflict — and how these are navigated through negotiated frameworks.

modes.reason: This node integrates the cultural obligations (Node 1) and the specific repatriation case (Node 2) into the descriptor's full demand: an understanding of how collaboration between First Nations Australians and other individuals and groups — including institutions and international bodies — functions to ensure cultural preservation. Students must coordinate the relational obligations, the specific example, and the institutional mechanisms into a coherent account.

descriptors.title: Historical and archaeological evidence
descriptors.description: the different methods and sources of evidence used by historians and archaeologists to investigate early societies, and the importance of archaeology and conserving the remains, material culture and heritage of the past
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain the cultural obligations of First Nations Australians regarding heritage sites and ancestral remains, and describe how collaboration between Traditional Owners and researchers supports cultural preservation (AC9HH7K07). Students also bring prior understanding of evidence types from AC9HH7K01 (stratigraphy, radiocarbon dating, oral history as evidence for early human migration). They have not yet examined the full range of methods used to investigate early (ancient) societies, nor the specific roles of archaeology and heritage conservation in that investigation.
elaborations: evaluating various methods for investigating the ancient past; for example, stratigraphy to date discoveries, and DNA testing to identify common diseases and past individuals from their remains, such as Egyptian mummies

creating a cross-sectional drawing of the earth's surface from an archaeological excavation to identify the evidence located at various layers (stratigraphy) and what it reveals about change over time; for example, a charcoal layer containing human remains and weapons may indicate the capture and destruction of an ancient settlement such as Troy
examining the impact of modern infrastructure works, such as the Aswan Dam, on sites of ancient significance

examining the roles and responsibilities of governments and other bodies, such as UNESCO, in protecting key archaeological sites; for example, the rescue mission to save the temples of Abu Simbel or the campaign for the return of the Elgin Marbles to Greece
investigating world heritage criteria for the listing of significant sites; for example, the Great Wall of China or the Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor (Qin Shi Huang) or Mohenjo-dara in India

nodes.label: Archaeological methods — stratigraphy and physical evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe stratigraphy as an archaeological method, explain how it is used to date discoveries and interpret change over time, and describe how physical evidence (artefacts, human remains) contributes to understanding early societies.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand stratigraphic logic — deeper = older, layer contents reveal activity at that time — cannot interpret how physical evidence within layers supports interpretations. N2 and N3 assume students can read layered evidence before adding DNA and written sources alongside it.
criteria: Explains stratigraphy correctly — deeper layers are older, layer contents reveal what was happening at that time.
Describes how specific evidence within a layer (human remains, weapons, charcoal) supports an interpretation of an event.
Does not treat stratigraphy as simply 'digging things up' — recognises it as a systematic method for reading change over time.

width.minimum: Describe stratigraphy as the analysis of earth layers to date and interpret archaeological finds, and explain how the depth of a find relates to its age.
width.typical: Describe stratigraphy as an archaeological method — how layers of sediment are read to establish chronology — and explain how physical evidence within those layers (human remains, weapons, charcoal, pottery) is used to interpret events and change over time. Use a specific example, such as a charcoal layer containing human remains and weapons indicating the capture and destruction of a settlement (e.g. Troy).
wider: Examine how a cross-sectional drawing of an archaeological excavation represents stratigraphic layers, and what specific evidence types found at different layers can reveal — connecting the visual representation to the interpretive practice.

Investigate the limitations of stratigraphy — including disturbance of layers by later activity, the challenge of establishing exact dates without additional dating methods, and what stratigraphy cannot tell us about why events happened.
Explore how stratigraphy was used at a specific ancient site to reconstruct its history — for example, the multiple occupation layers at Çatalhöyük or the stratigraphic evidence at Troy.

modes.reason: The logical structure of stratigraphic reading — deeper = older, layer contents = evidence of activity at that time, transitions between layers = change events — is non-obvious to Year 7 students. Without explicit scaffolding of this reasoning chain, students cannot construct or interpret a cross-sectional diagram or understand why a charcoal layer with weapons indicates destruction rather than simply 'things were buried here'.

nodes.label: Scientific methods — DNA testing and dating techniques
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe DNA testing and dating techniques (such as radiocarbon dating) as scientific methods used alongside archaeology to investigate early societies, and identify what each method can and cannot reveal.
criteria: Describes DNA testing and identifies at least one type of information it can provide about ancient individuals or populations.
Distinguishes DNA testing from stratigraphy — recognises them as different methods providing different types of evidence.
Explains that dating techniques provide estimates within error ranges, not exact dates — uncertainty is intrinsic to the method.

width.minimum: Describe DNA testing as a method for identifying individuals or tracing population relationships from ancient remains, and identify one thing it can reveal (e.g. disease history, individual identity, population movement).
width.typical: Describe DNA testing and dating techniques as complementary scientific methods — explaining what DNA analysis of ancient remains (e.g. Egyptian mummies, ancient skeletal material) can reveal about individuals, disease, and population relationships, and how radiocarbon dating establishes the age of organic material. Explain that these methods work alongside stratigraphy and written sources rather than replacing them.
wider: Examine specific cases where DNA analysis has produced significant findings — for example, DNA testing of Egyptian royal mummies revealing family relationships and disease history, or ancient DNA analysis reshaping understanding of population migrations.

Investigate the limitations of each dating technique — the radiocarbon dating error range, what radiocarbon cannot date (inorganic material), and the conditions required for DNA preservation in ancient remains.
Explore how advances in ancient DNA technology (aDNA) have transformed our understanding of ancient societies in the past decade, including what was previously unknowable and is now accessible.

modes.reason: Students encounter DNA testing and radiocarbon dating as new method types alongside stratigraphy — not just additional depth on the same method. Exposure to how each method type addresses different questions (who was this person vs when was this layer deposited vs what was written at the time) builds the understanding that a repertoire of complementary methods is required for robust archaeological interpretation.

nodes.label: Written sources and the challenges of ancient evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the role of written sources in investigating early societies, identify challenges in interpreting ancient written sources (including translation and intercultural understanding), and explain how historians triangulate across multiple source types.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat written sources as automatically more reliable than physical or oral evidence will apply a flawed reliability hierarchy in S03–S04, producing source assessments that privilege text without critical analysis — undermining the triangulation principle that underpins sound historical inquiry.
criteria: Names at least one type of ancient written source and identifies a specific challenge in using it as historical evidence.
Explains that historians triangulate across multiple source types rather than relying on a single source.
Does not treat written sources as automatically more reliable than physical or oral evidence.

width.minimum: Identify at least one type of written source used to investigate early societies (e.g. inscriptions, religious texts, edicts) and describe one challenge in interpreting it (e.g. translation difficulties, cultural context).
width.typical: Describe the role of written sources — including inscriptions, edicts (e.g. Asoka's edicts), and religious literature (e.g. the Vedas, Ramayana, Mahabharata) — in investigating early societies, and explain the challenges these sources present: translation difficulties, intercultural understanding, distinguishing religious/literary intent from historical description. Explain how historians use multiple source types together rather than relying on any single source.
wider: Investigate specific cases of translation challenge — such as the decipherment of Linear B, the Rosetta Stone, or the challenges of reading Asoka's edicts in multiple scripts — examining what the translation process itself reveals about ancient communication and scholarship.

Examine the distinction between primary sources from ancient societies (inscriptions, texts from the time) and secondary sources (modern historical interpretations), and how this distinction shapes how historians assess reliability.

Explore what the absence of written sources means for our understanding of societies without writing — examining how this shapes what questions can and cannot be answered about pre-literate societies.

modes.reason: Students commonly treat written sources as automatically more reliable than physical or oral evidence. Examining multiple written source types — each with different translation challenges, different purposes, and different relationships to historical reality — specifically dislodges this bias. Breadth across source types (inscriptions, religious epics, administrative edicts) builds the understanding that all sources require critical interpretation.

nodes.label: Importance of conservation — archaeology and heritage
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why the conservation of archaeological sites, remains, material culture, and heritage is important, and describe the roles of governments and international bodies (e.g. UNESCO) in protecting significant sites.
criteria: Explains why conservation matters — that lost evidence cannot be recovered and that the past is irreplaceable.
Identifies at least one specific threat to heritage sites (infrastructure, looting, neglect) and one protective mechanism (UNESCO, national legislation).
Describes at least one specific case — Abu Simbel, Elgin Marbles, or a world heritage site — in the context of conservation or repatriation.

width.minimum: Explain why conservation of archaeological remains and heritage sites matters — that once destroyed, evidence cannot be recovered — and identify one role that governments or international bodies play in protection.
width.typical: Explain the importance of archaeological conservation — that irreplaceable evidence is at risk from infrastructure development, looting, and neglect — and describe the roles of governments and bodies such as UNESCO in protecting sites. Use specific examples: the impact of the Aswan Dam on ancient Egyptian sites, the rescue of the temples of Abu Simbel, and the debate over the Elgin Marbles.
wider: Examine the Abu Simbel rescue mission in detail — the scale of the engineering involved in moving the temples, what drove the decision, and what was at stake — as a case study in international collaboration for heritage conservation.

Investigate the Elgin Marbles debate — the circumstances of their removal, the arguments for and against return, and the broader questions about who owns ancient heritage — as an ongoing contemporary controversy.

Explore world heritage listing criteria and how sites such as the Great Wall of China, the Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor, and Mohenjo-daro satisfy them, connecting to the parallel world heritage discussion in K07.

modes.reason: This node integrates all three evidence method nodes into the descriptor's final demand — understanding why the methods, the sources, and the sites they investigate matter enough to conserve. Students must connect the value of archaeological evidence (Nodes 1–3) to the ethical and practical imperative to protect it. Conservation is the 'so what' that completes the descriptor's arc.

descriptors.title: Environment and ancient development
descriptors.description: how the physical environment and geographical features influenced the development of the ancient society
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the methods and sources of evidence used by historians and archaeologists to investigate early societies, and explain the importance of conservation (AC9HH7K08). They have not yet examined how the physical environment and geography specifically shaped the development of an ancient society — the cause-and-effect relationship between landscape and civilisation.
elaborations: explaining the role of topography in providing barriers of defence for city-states, such as the surrounding seas, mountain ranges and river systems; for example, the Axios (Vardar), Strimonas (Struma) and Nestos rivers
