nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the role of the chosen individual or group in their specific historical context — including the conditions that enabled their influence — drawing on primary and secondary sources as evidence.
criteria: Describes the role of the chosen individual or group using at least one primary or secondary source as evidence
Explains at least one condition (social, political, religious or economic) that enabled the individual or group to exercise influence

width.minimum: A description of the chosen individual or group's role with at least one source as evidence.
width.typical: A well-contextualised account of the role — including the social, political or religious conditions that enabled it — using multiple sources; the role of the Catholic Church in provision of social services, education and feudal organisation; or the influence of Renaissance patrons such as the Medici family; or political figures such as Henry VIII, Elizabeth I, Martin Luther or Louis XIV.
wider: Use visual sources such as the illustration of Hell in the Hortus Deliciarum (Herrad of Landsberg) to examine the Church's role in shaping beliefs and social control
Examine Lucrezia Borgia as a case study in how gender, political alliance and historiography intersect in assessing a significant individual's role

modes.reason: The range of possible subjects for this standard is very wide — Church, Medici, scientific figures, political reformers. Varying the type of source used (visual, written, architectural) helps students see that historical role can be evidenced in multiple ways.

nodes.label: Achievements and their impact
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the achievements of the chosen individual or group and describe their impact on contemporaries and on later developments.
criteria: Identifies at least two achievements of the chosen individual or group
Explains the impact of at least one achievement on contemporaries and on later historical developments

width.minimum: At least two achievements of the chosen individual or group with an explanation of their impact.
width.typical: Multiple achievements analysed for both immediate and longer-term impact; the Scientific Revolution as a case study in how individual discoveries (Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler, Newton) collectively overturned traditional views and contributed to science as an alternative to Church authority; Oliver Cromwell's role in the English Civil War and parliamentary development.
wider: Examine the importance of the Scientific Revolution — particularly how Copernicus, Galileo and Newton's theories overturned traditional views of planetary motion — and how this contributed to science being seen as an alternative to the Church as a source of truth

Investigate how the significance of Oliver Cromwell and the execution of Charles I contributed to the development of the Westminster parliamentary system, tracing achievement through to modern institutions

modes.reason: Students often list achievements without connecting them to impact. Scaffold the logic: achievement X had impact Y on contemporaries, and its longer-term legacy was Z. Each achievement needs an explicitly reasoned chain of consequence.

nodes.label: Legacy and historical judgement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the legacy of the chosen individual or group — explaining what endured from their achievements and how historians have judged their significance — and connect this legacy to the development of the modern world.
criteria: Explains at least one lasting legacy of the chosen individual or group and connects it to a feature of the modern world
Evaluates the significance of the individual or group using evidence, not just assertion

width.minimum: An explanation of at least one lasting legacy of the chosen individual or group and a connection to a feature of the modern world.
width.typical: Legacy assessed through multiple criteria; how historians' judgements of significance have changed over time; the enduring impact of the Catholic Church, the Medici, key Enlightenment figures or scientific revolutionaries on modern political, religious or intellectual life.
wider: Examine how the influences and contributions of individuals such as Machiavelli, Luther or Louis XIV have been reinterpreted across different historical periods, showing that legacy is not fixed

Investigate why the achievements of women such as Lucrezia Borgia or Elizabeth I have historically been undervalued or misrepresented, connecting this to historiographical questions about who is deemed significant

modes.reason: Legacy assessment integrates significance criteria (Node 1), contextual role (Node 2) and impact analysis (Node 3). Invest in helping students articulate a coherent historical judgement that draws on all three rather than treating legacy as a separate summary.

descriptors.title: Interpretations of medieval Europe
descriptors.description: interpretations about an event, individual, group, institution or movement in Medieval, Renaissance or pre-modern Europe
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain historical interpretations about significant events, individuals and groups in ancient contexts (AC9HH7K — implicit from prior band) and have developed skills in source analysis (AC9HH7S07). They have not yet examined how and why historians construct different interpretations of the same medieval or early modern subject, including how myths, misconceptions and changing access to sources shape historical understanding.
elaborations: explaining how historians have disproved medieval myths such as King Arthur or Pope Joan
analysing why the Black Death has been misconceived as impacting Europe predominantly, with reference to differing historians' interpretations

analysing the importance of key women in Renaissance society, such as Caterina Sforza (1463–1509), Isabella d'Este (1474–1539), Lucrezia Borgia (1480–1519) and Catherine de Medici (1519–1589), using a range of artwork, written sources and historians' interpretations to justify claims
The emergence of the modern world

explaining how the interpretations of the discoveries of science are linked to ideas about the free exercise of human reason and how that could lead to improvements and progress in human life and society generally

examining historical interpretations of key events, developments or achievements during this period, such as the Scientific Revolution or the beginnings of the Age of Reason/Enlightenment, and how these interpretations highlight their importance or significance to contemporary society

nodes.label: What is a historical interpretation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the difference between historical fact and historical interpretation, and describe why the same event or individual can be interpreted differently by different historians.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish between fact and interpretation, or who treat historical accounts as simply true or false, cannot analyse competing interpretations. The conceptual distinction is necessary for all subsequent nodes.
criteria: Explains the difference between a historical fact and a historical interpretation using a specific medieval or early modern example
Identifies at least one reason why historians might interpret the same event or individual differently

width.minimum: An explanation of the distinction between fact and interpretation applied to one medieval or early modern subject.
width.typical: The concept of historical interpretation — how historians use evidence, personal perspective, and the context in which they work to construct accounts; the distinction between myth/legend and historical evidence (e.g. King Arthur, Pope Joan) as a clear illustration of why interpretation must be grounded in evidence.
wider: Examine how historians have disproved medieval myths such as King Arthur or Pope Joan, showing how new evidence and rigorous method change interpretations

Explore how the interpretations of the Scientific Revolution or the Enlightenment have changed over time — from being seen as purely European achievements to being understood in a broader intercultural context

modes.reason: The fact/interpretation distinction is deceptively simple — students need explicit scaffolding to understand that interpretation is not just opinion but a reasoned, evidence-based account that can be evaluated. Use concrete medieval examples (myths vs documented history) to make the distinction tangible.

nodes.label: Competing interpretations and why they differ
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe competing historical interpretations of a chosen subject and explain why historians have reached different conclusions — including differences in access to sources, personal perspective, and the historical context in which historians worked.
criteria: Describes at least two different historical interpretations of the chosen subject
Explains at least one reason why the interpretations differ (e.g. access to sources, perspective, historical context of the historian)

width.minimum: Two different interpretations of the chosen subject with at least one explanation of why they differ.
width.typical: Multiple competing interpretations analysed for their evidentiary basis and the factors that shaped them; the Black Death as misconceived as primarily a European event; contrasting perspectives on the role of women in Renaissance society; the 'Gold, God and Glory' framework for Spanish conquest as a contested interpretation.
wider: Analyse the importance of key women in Renaissance society — Caterina Sforza, Isabella d'Este, Lucrezia Borgia, Catherine de Medici — using artwork, written sources and historians' interpretations to examine how gendered assumptions shaped historical accounts
Examine why the Black Death has been misconceived as predominantly European, with reference to differing historians' interpretations and evidence from affected regions in Asia and the Middle East

modes.reason: The range of medieval subjects for which competing interpretations exist is wide. Using multiple subjects (Black Death, Renaissance women, Scientific Revolution) prevents students from treating interpretation as specific to one case and helps them see it as a general feature of historical knowledge.

nodes.label: Evaluating interpretations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate historical interpretations by examining the evidence they rest on and identifying factors that might limit or strengthen them.
criteria: Evaluates at least one historical interpretation by identifying evidence that supports or limits it
Explains how factors such as source availability, perspective or historical context affect the strength of an interpretation

width.minimum: An evaluation of at least one interpretation using evidence to assess its strengths or limitations.
width.typical: Evaluation of competing interpretations using source evidence; how discoveries of science are linked to ideas about the free exercise of human reason; how the importance or significance of the Scientific Revolution or Enlightenment is highlighted or questioned depending on the interpretive lens used.
wider: Examine how the interpretations of the Enlightenment and Scientific Revolution highlight their importance to contemporary society, evaluating how much weight to give modern relevance as a criterion in judging historical significance

Analyse how modern historians' interpretations of the Crusades differ depending on whether they focus on European, Islamic or Byzantine perspectives — and evaluate which interpretation is best supported by the available evidence

modes.reason: Students need a method for evaluating interpretations — not just noting that they differ but asking which is better supported, by what evidence, and why. Scaffold the evaluation process explicitly: identify the claim, identify the evidence, assess the strength of the link.

descriptors.title: Features of empire and expansion
descriptors.description: the significant social, religious, cultural, economic, environmental and/or political features of different groups related to the empire and/or expansion
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain the significant social, religious, cultural, economic and political features of ancient societies (AC9HH7K09, AC9HH7K11). They understand how to describe the organisation of a society across multiple dimensions. They have not yet examined these features in the context of medieval empires and expansionist societies — the Mongols, Ottomans, Vikings or the Spanish conquest of the Americas.
elaborations: describing the nomadic nature of Mongol life and how it enabled the rise of Temujin (Genghis Khan), who united all Mongol tribes in 1206 CE

describing facets of life in Mongolia and the incorporation of these facets into Chinese life; for example, agriculture – domestication of animals such as horses, camels and cattle; food – dried meat and yoghurt; housing – yurts

describing the way of life of people in the Ottoman Empire; for example, the role of women, the role of the coffee house and bazaar or marketplace, and the power and responsibility of the Sultan to ensure that justice was served within society
using a selection of primary sources to track changes in the way of life in the Ottoman Empire across time or locations

describing the way of life of the Vikings; for example, living in a cold and harsh environment, the importance of farming and raids, the significance of honour in Viking warrior society and the role of gender
explaining how the environment of Viking lands in Scandinavia influenced the activities of societies
The Spanish conquest of the Americas

describing pre-Columbian life in the Americas, including the social organisation of the Aztecs (for example, nobility and slaves), their beliefs (for example, worship of a number of gods and the need to make human sacrifices to appease these gods), and life in the capital city of Tenochtitlan

nodes.label: Way of life and social organisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the way of life and social organisation of the chosen group — including how their environment, economy and social structure shaped their daily existence.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding the way of life of the chosen group — how their environment, economy and social structure shaped them — students cannot explain why they expanded, how they governed, or what the effects of expansion were. The social foundation is prerequisite to all subsequent nodes.
criteria: Describes at least two features of the chosen group's way of life using historically specific detail
Explains how at least one environmental or economic factor shaped the group's social organisation

width.minimum: A description of at least two features of the chosen group's way of life (e.g. social roles, food, housing, gender roles) grounded in the specific historical context.
width.typical: Multiple features of daily life across social, economic and environmental dimensions, grounded in primary source evidence where possible. Examples: the nomadic nature of Mongol life and its role in enabling Genghis Khan's rise; the role of the coffee house, bazaar and Sultan's authority in Ottoman society; Viking living conditions, farming, raiding, and the significance of honour; pre-Columbian Aztec society including nobility, slavery, religious beliefs and Tenochtitlan.
wider: For the Mongols: examine how facets of Mongol life (horses, camels, yurts, dried meat) were incorporated into Chinese life after conquest, showing how expansion transformed both the conquerors and the conquered
For the Vikings: investigate how the environment of Scandinavian Viking lands directly influenced the activities — farming limitations, coastal access, shipbuilding — that drove expansion
For the Ottomans: use primary sources to track changes in way of life across different times or locations within the Ottoman Empire, showing variation within the empire

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate specific, concrete details of the chosen group's way of life before they can generalise about social features. One or two facts are insufficient — build a rich picture across social, economic, environmental and cultural dimensions.

nodes.label: Religious and cultural features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the religious beliefs and cultural practices of the chosen group and explain how these shaped social order, motivated action and enabled or constrained expansion.
criteria: Describes at least one religious or cultural feature of the chosen group with historically specific detail
Explains how that feature shaped social order or contributed to the group's expansion or governance

width.minimum: A description of at least one religious or cultural feature and its role in the chosen group's society or expansion.
width.typical: Religious and cultural features examined in relation to their social function and expansionist role. Examples: the significance of honour and warrior culture in Viking society; the Ottoman system of justice and religious tolerance; Mongol religious plurality; Aztec polytheism, human sacrifice and its social/political functions; the role of Christian missionary motivation in Spanish conquest.
wider: For the Vikings: identify the key roles of gods such as Odin, Thor, Frey and Freyja in Viking religion and the impact of the adoption of Christianity during the Viking period on social and cultural continuity
For the Aztecs: examine the social and political functions of religious practices (e.g. human sacrifice as state ritual) to understand how religion underwrote political authority in Tenochtitlan

modes.reason: Religious and cultural features vary widely across the possible subjects. Using more than one religious context (e.g. Islamic, polytheistic, Christian) prevents students from generalising from a single case.

nodes.label: Economic and environmental features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the economic activities and environmental context of the chosen group and explain how these shaped their expansion and interactions with other societies.
criteria: Describes at least one economic activity of the chosen group and explains its connection to their expansion or wider influence
Identifies how an environmental feature shaped the group's economic or expansionist capacity

width.minimum: A description of at least one economic activity and its relationship to the group's expansion or influence.
width.typical: Economic and environmental features across trade, agriculture, resource use and technology. Examples: Mongol trade networks connecting Europe and Asia; Ottoman bazaars and trade routes; Viking longboat technology enabling trade and raiding; Aztec agriculture and resource management in Tenochtitlan; Spanish conquest driven by access to American commodities.
wider: For the Ottomans: examine inventions and developments in the Islamic world (astrolabe, public hospitals and libraries) and their adoption in the Western world, showing how economic and intellectual expansion intersected
For the Vikings: investigate the construction of longboats — innovations in keel and sail design — as a case study in how technological development enabled economic and military expansion

modes.reason: Students need to see the link between economic capacity (trade, technology, agriculture) and the ability to expand. Scaffold the reasoning: what resources or technologies did this group have, and how did these enable or constrain their expansion?

descriptors.title: Turning points in empire and expansion
descriptors.description: a significant event, development, turning point or challenge that contributed to continuity and change related to the empire and/or expansion
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain the causes and effects of contacts and conflicts within and between ancient societies (AC9HH7K12) and understand the concept of turning points from prior study (AC9HH8K03). They understand the social and cultural features of the chosen empire (AC9HH8K07). They have not yet applied turning point analysis to the specific context of empire and expansion.
elaborations: explaining the role of the Mongols in forging connections between Europe and Asia through conquest, settlement and trade; for example, the use of paper money and coinage; the growing number of European merchants travelling to China

explaining Genghis Khan's use of decimal organisation in his army and his policies for governing his empire, including codifying laws, banning the killing of animals in the breeding season, supporting religious freedom and expanding trade
analysing the effects of Mongol expansion including life in China before, during and after the Mongol conquest
explaining the role of warfare in expanding Ottoman territory, including the sieges of Bursa (1317–1326 CE) and Nicaea (1328–1331 CE)
describing Ottoman art and architecture, such as Selimiye Mosque in the city of Edirne in Turkey, and Islamic geometric design
outlining inventions and developments in the Islamic world, such as the astrolabe, public hospitals and libraries, and their subsequent adoption in the Western world
explaining the impact of the Crusades in challenging the Ottoman Empire and the responses of the Ottomans to the challenge
identifying the key role of gods such as Odin, Thor, Frey and Freyja in Viking religion and the impact of the adoption of Christianity during the Viking period
explaining the significance of the construction of longboats and their role in exploration, including innovations in keel and sail design
identifying and analysing evidence of Viking trade between Russia (Kiev) and the east (through Constantinople)
describing Viking craft with particular emphasis on the production of weapons and armour (for example, swords, battle axes and helmets) and the effectiveness of these in battle
explaining the triggers of declining Viking power such as the Battle of Standford Bridge, the treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, new colonies, changing climate and/or the spread of Christianity
The Spanish conquest of the Americas

explaining the arrival of Spanish conquistadores in Mexico and Peru from 1510 CE (Balboa) to 1531 (Pizarro), and their reasons; for example, seeking wealth, claiming land for their king, converting the local populations to Christianity, sense of adventure
analysing the significance of Alexander VI's papal decrees of 1493 in legalising Spanish territorial expansion and claims in the Americas

outlining the effects of Spanish conquest on the Americas, such as the spread of disease, introduction of crops such as maize, beans, tobacco, chocolate and potatoes to Europe, the Encomienda system, mining and deforestation, and the impact of the loss of natural resources

explaining the longer-term effects of conquest and colonisation on the Indigenous populations of the Americas, such as the unequal distribution of land and wealth, slavery, political inequality, and supremacy of Spanish culture and language over conquered territories

nodes.label: The turning point in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a significant turning point in the context of the chosen empire or expansion and explain how it fits within the broader trajectory of that society's development.
criteria: Identifies a specific turning point in the chosen empire or expansion and explains its place in the broader historical trajectory
Distinguishes between the turning point as an event and the longer-term conditions that enabled it

width.minimum: Identification of a specific turning point with an explanation of its place in the empire's or expansion's history.
width.typical: The turning point situated within the empire's broader arc. Examples: Genghis Khan's unification of Mongol tribes (1206) enabling conquest; Ottoman sieges of Bursa and Nicaea establishing territorial expansion; the Battle of Standford Bridge or the spread of Christianity as triggers of Viking decline; Alexander VI's papal decrees (1493) legalising Spanish expansion in the Americas.
wider: For the Mongols: compare the unification under Genghis Khan with the reign of Kublai Khan as two turning points — one enabling expansion, one managing its consequences — to show how turning points can have different characters

For the Spanish conquest: examine the significance of Alexander VI's papal decrees (1493) as both a political and religious turning point that simultaneously legitimised territorial expansion and framed it as a religious mission

modes.reason: Students need to situate the turning point within the empire's trajectory before they can analyse its causes and effects. Scaffold the contextualisation: what was happening before, what changed with this event, and what was the subsequent direction?

nodes.label: Causes and features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the causes and key features of the chosen turning point, using primary and secondary sources as evidence.
nodes.hinge_reason: A well-evidenced causal account of the turning point is prerequisite to analysing its effects on continuity and change. Students who cannot describe what happened and why cannot explain what it changed.
criteria: Identifies at least two causes of the turning point, distinguishing between immediate triggers and longer-term conditions
Describes the key features of the turning point using at least one source as evidence

width.minimum: At least two causes and a description of the key features of the turning point, with reference to at least one source.
width.typical: Multiple causes (immediate and longer-term) with detailed description of key features. Examples: Genghis Khan's use of decimal organisation, codified laws and religious freedom policies as features of a governing turning point; Ottoman warfare and architectural achievements (Selimiye Mosque) as features of expansion; the construction of Viking longboats — keel and sail innovations — as a technological turning point enabling expansion; the arrival of Spanish conquistadores from 1510 (Balboa) through 1531 (Pizarro) and their motivations.
wider: For the Mongols: examine Genghis Khan's policies (banning seasonal animal killing, supporting religious freedom, expanding trade) as evidence of a governing philosophy that made the empire administratively sustainable
For the Vikings: investigate evidence of Viking trade between Russia (Kiev) and the east through Constantinople as evidence of a turning point from raiding culture to trading civilisation
For the Ottoman Empire: analyse the impact of the Crusades as a challenge to Ottoman expansion and examine Ottoman responses as features of the turning point

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate sufficient source-based detail about the turning point before they can make well-supported causal claims. Prioritise depth of evidence — the more specific and grounded the account, the stronger the subsequent analysis.

nodes.label: Effects on continuity and change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the effects of the turning point on the empire or expansion — describing what changed and what continued — for different groups including rulers, subject peoples and affected societies.
criteria: Explains at least one change and one continuity resulting from the turning point, with reference to specific evidence
Describes how the turning point affected at least two different groups differently

width.minimum: At least two effects (one change and one continuity) with reference to at least one affected group.
width.typical: Multiple effects across social, economic, religious and political domains; different effects for different groups; longer-term consequences. Examples: Mongol expansion effects — connections between Europe and Asia, paper money, European merchant travel to China; Spanish conquest effects — spread of disease, introduction of American crops to Europe, the Encomienda system, deforestation, longer-term inequality and cultural displacement of Indigenous populations.
wider: For the Spanish conquest: analyse longer-term effects on Indigenous populations — unequal land distribution, slavery, political inequality, supremacy of Spanish culture and language — to show how a medieval turning point produced modern inequalities

For the Vikings: examine the decline of Viking power (Battle of Standford Bridge, treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, changing climate, spread of Christianity) as a multi-causal chain of continuity and change

For the Mongols: analyse the effects of Mongol expansion including life in China before, during and after conquest to show how the same turning point produced different continuities and changes in different places

modes.reason: Effects of empire and expansion are always unequal — what changed for the conquerors often differed dramatically from what changed for the conquered. Using multiple group perspectives (rulers, subject peoples, distant affected societies) builds a fuller analysis.

descriptors.title: Power and authority in empire
descriptors.description: the experiences and perspectives of rulers and of subject peoples, and how the interaction between power and/or authority relates to the empire and/or expansion
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how power and authority operated in medieval Europe (AC9HH8K04) and the social and cultural features of the chosen empire (AC9HH8K07). They have not yet analysed the specific power structures and relationships between rulers and subject peoples in the context of empire and expansion.
elaborations: describing the reign of Kublai Khan as the first Mongol emperor of China (the Yuan Dynasty), including the processes of government using administrators from different backgrounds and the growth of Chinese culture during this time
explaining the role of the Mongols in forging connections between Europe and Asia through conquest, settlement and trade, for example the meeting of Marco Polo and the development of trade
outlining the millet system that regarded non-Muslim people as subjects but as not being subject to Muslim law
explaining the tolerance of the Ottomans towards Christians and Jews
explaining the attacks on monasteries such as Lindisfarne (793 CE) and Iona (795 CE) and reviewing the written accounts of monks that contributed to the Vikings' reputation for pillaging and violence

explaining the survival of a heroic Iron Age society in early Medieval Ireland, as described in the vernacular epics, and its transformation by the spread of Christianity, the influence of the Vikings and the Anglo-Norman conquest
investigating the remains of Viking settlements such as Dublin (Ireland) and Jorvik (York)
The Spanish conquest of the Americas
describing encounters between Hernán Cortés and the Aztecs, as well as the siege of Tenochtitlan

investigating the impact of conquest on the Indigenous populations of the Americas (for example, the introduction of new diseases, horses and gunpowder, and the loss of natural resources) and the wider world (for example, the introduction of crops such as maize, beans, potatoes, tobacco and chocolate from the Americas to Europe and increased wealth in Europe)

nodes.label: How rulers exercised power
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how rulers in the chosen empire exercised power — including through governance systems, military force, religious authority and symbolic legitimacy — and explain how these mechanisms sustained their rule.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how power was exercised is prerequisite to understanding how subject peoples experienced and responded to it. Students who cannot explain the mechanisms of imperial rule cannot analyse the perspectives of those ruled.
criteria: Identifies at least two mechanisms through which the chosen ruler exercised power and explains how they sustained authority
Distinguishes between how power was established (conquest) and how it was maintained (governance)

width.minimum: At least two mechanisms through which the chosen ruler exercised power, with a brief explanation of how they sustained authority.
width.typical: Multiple mechanisms of imperial rule. Examples: Kublai Khan as first Mongol emperor of China (Yuan Dynasty) — use of administrators from diverse backgrounds, growth of Chinese culture; the Ottoman Sultan's responsibility for justice; the millet system's governance of non-Muslim subjects; Cortés and the siege of Tenochtitlan as a display of military power transforming political authority.
wider: For the Mongols: examine the role of Marco Polo and the development of trade as evidence of how Mongol rulers used economic connections as well as military conquest to consolidate power

For the Ottomans: analyse the millet system — which regarded non-Muslim people as subjects but not subject to Muslim law — as a case study in how religious plurality was managed as a governance strategy

modes.reason: Students often conflate conquest with governance. Scaffold the distinction: how did rulers maintain power after expansion? The mechanisms of ongoing governance (administration, law, religious tolerance, trade) are different from the mechanisms of military conquest.

nodes.label: Experiences of subject peoples
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the experiences and perspectives of subject peoples under the chosen empire — including how conquest, governance and cultural contact affected their daily lives — and explain how these experiences differed across groups.
criteria: Describes the experience of at least one subject group under the chosen empire using historically specific detail
Identifies at least one way in which the experience of different subject groups differed within the same empire

width.minimum: A description of the experience of at least one subject group with reference to how imperial rule affected their daily life.
width.typical: Varied experiences of subject peoples across different groups. Examples: Ottoman tolerance of Christians and Jews vs the constraints of dhimmi status; Viking attacks on monasteries (Lindisfarne 793 CE, Iona 795 CE) experienced from the monks' written perspective; Aztec subjects under Spanish conquest — introduction of disease, horses, gunpowder, loss of resources; survival of Iron Age society in early medieval Ireland transformed by Christianity, Vikings and Anglo-Norman conquest.
wider: For the Vikings: examine the written accounts of monks that contributed to the Vikings' reputation for pillaging — and question how this single-perspective source shapes historical understanding of Viking-subject encounters

For the Spanish conquest: investigate the impact of conquest on Indigenous populations (disease, horses, gunpowder, loss of natural resources) and the introduction of American crops to Europe, examining both sides of the colonial exchange

modes.reason: The experience of subject peoples is highly variable across empires and within them. Using multiple subject groups (e.g. Ottoman dhimmi vs Aztec commoners under Spanish rule) prevents students from generalising from a single subordinate experience.

nodes.label: Interactions between power and resistance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how subject peoples responded to imperial power — through accommodation, resistance, or cultural exchange — and explain how these interactions shaped the development of the empire or expansion.
criteria: Identifies at least one example of how subject peoples responded to imperial power
Explains how that response — accommodation, resistance or exchange — affected the development of the empire

width.minimum: At least one example of how subject peoples responded to imperial power (accommodation, resistance or exchange) with an explanation of its effect.
width.typical: Responses across accommodation, resistance and exchange. Examples: the forging of connections between Europe and Asia through Mongol trade (Marco Polo); the survival and transformation of Irish society through Viking and Norman contact; the Aztec responses to Cortés including the siege of Tenochtitlan; Viking settlements in Dublin (Ireland) and Jorvik (York) as evidence of cultural integration as well as conquest.
wider: Examine the remains of Viking settlements such as Dublin and Jorvik as archaeological evidence of cultural integration — settlements showing how 'conquerors' and 'subject peoples' created hybrid societies

For the Spanish conquest: investigate the encounters between Cortés and the Aztecs, examining how Aztec responses to Spanish power — including alliances with rival indigenous groups — shaped the outcome of the conquest

modes.reason: Students tend to frame subject-empire interactions as purely one-directional (conquerors act, subjects suffer). Scaffold the analysis to include how subject peoples' responses shaped the empire — trade relationships, cultural borrowing, resistance that forced governance adaptation.

descriptors.title: Significant individuals in empire
descriptors.description: the role and achievements of a significant individual and/or group connected to the empire and/or expansion
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain the role and achievements of a significant individual in an ancient society (AC9HH7K13) and understand significance as a historical concept (AC9HH8K05). They understand the social and cultural features of the chosen empire (AC9HH8K07) and its turning points (AC9HH8K08). They have not yet applied significance analysis to individuals specifically connected to medieval empire and expansion.
elaborations: identifying the similarities in leadership styles and successes of Genghis Khan and Kublai Khan

comparing historians' interpretations of the achievements of individuals such as Selim I in establishing the empire and capturing Jerusalem, or Suleiman the Magnificent in expanding the empire to Belgrade in Europe
outlining Erik the Red's development of Viking settlements in Eastern and Western Greenland in 985 CE

comparing the artefacts discovered at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland (Canada) with Viking artefacts as possible evidence that the Vikings had journeyed to North America 500 years before Christopher Columbus
The Spanish conquest of the Americas
explaining the significance of key chronological events in the lives of individuals such as Columbus, Balboa, Cortés, Montezuma II and/or Pizarro

nodes.label: The individual in historical context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the historical context in which the chosen individual operated and explain the conditions that enabled their rise to significance.
criteria: Describes the role of the chosen individual in the context of the chosen empire or expansion
Explains at least one condition (social, military, political or cultural) that enabled the individual's rise to significance

width.minimum: A description of the chosen individual's role with reference to the conditions that enabled it.
width.typical: The chosen individual situated within the empire's broader context. Examples: Genghis Khan's unification of Mongol tribes enabled by their nomadic military culture; Kublai Khan as first Mongol emperor of China, his administrative approach and relationship to Chinese culture; Selim I capturing Jerusalem or Suleiman the Magnificent expanding to Belgrade; Erik the Red's settlement of Greenland; Columbus, Balboa, Cortés, Montezuma II or Pizarro in the chronology of Spanish conquest.
wider: Compare the leadership styles and successes of Genghis Khan and Kublai Khan — military expansion vs administrative consolidation — to show how different approaches to power can both be significant
Examine the artefacts at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland as possible evidence that the Vikings journeyed to North America 500 years before Columbus, questioning who 'discovered' the Americas

modes.reason: Students often attribute empire-building to individual greatness without examining the conditions that made individuals' actions possible. Scaffold the contextualisation: what circumstances enabled this person to act as they did?

nodes.label: Achievements and their significance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the key achievements of the chosen individual and evaluate their significance — describing both what was achieved and why it mattered for the empire and for later history.
nodes.hinge_reason: Achievement analysis is the core demand of this descriptor. Students who cannot explain what was achieved and why it mattered — rather than merely narrating events — have not met the standard. Legacy analysis in the next node depends on solid achievement analysis here.
criteria: Identifies at least two achievements of the chosen individual
Explains why each achievement was significant — not just what happened, but what it changed or enabled

width.minimum: At least two achievements of the chosen individual with an explanation of their significance.
width.typical: Multiple achievements analysed for immediate and longer-term significance. Examples: Genghis Khan's decimal military organisation, codified laws and policies; Selim I or Suleiman the Magnificent's territorial expansion and governance; Erik the Red's development of Viking settlements in Greenland; key chronological events in the lives of Columbus, Cortés or Pizarro and their significance for the Americas.
wider: Compare historians' interpretations of Selim I and Suleiman the Magnificent's achievements to show how the same individual's record can be assessed differently depending on the interpretive lens

Examine Erik the Red's development of Viking settlements in eastern and western Greenland (985 CE) as evidence of expansion beyond the known world — and compare with L'Anse aux Meadows to evaluate the extent of Viking achievement

modes.reason: Students often narrate a biography rather than analyse achievements. Scaffold the distinction: an achievement is not just something that happened but something that had consequence. Each achievement needs an explicitly reasoned explanation of why it mattered.

nodes.label: Legacy and historical judgement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the legacy of the chosen individual — explaining what endured from their achievements, how historians have judged their significance, and what their actions mean for our understanding of empire and expansion.
criteria: Explains at least one lasting legacy of the chosen individual and connects it to the empire's or expansion's longer-term history
References at least one historians' judgement and evaluates it against the evidence

width.minimum: An explanation of at least one lasting legacy and a reference to how the individual is regarded by historians.
width.typical: Legacy evaluated across multiple criteria; differing historians' perspectives on the individual's significance; connections between the individual's achievements and ongoing historical developments. Examples: the Mongol legacy in trade connections and cultural exchange; the Viking legacy in settlement and navigation; the contested legacy of Spanish conquest for Indigenous populations and for the modern world.
wider: Examine how historians' interpretations of conquistadores such as Cortés or Pizarro differ — from heroic explorers to colonial oppressors — as a case study in how the same individual can be judged very differently depending on whose perspective is centred
Compare the achievements of Genghis Khan and Kublai Khan across military conquest and cultural administration to evaluate which form of achievement has left a more enduring legacy

modes.reason: Legacy assessment integrates contextual understanding (Node 1) and achievement analysis (Node 2). Invest in helping students articulate a coherent historical judgement that draws on both, rather than treating legacy as a separate summary exercise.

descriptors.title: Interpretations of empire
descriptors.description: interpretations about the society and events, and/or individuals and/or groups connected to the empire and/or expansion
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how historians construct and evaluate interpretations (AC9HH8K06) and the events, individuals and society of the chosen empire (AC9HH8K07–K10). They have not yet applied interpretive analysis specifically to the contested historiography of medieval empires and expansion — including how oral traditions, primary sources, death tolls and post-colonial perspectives shape historical understanding.
elaborations: discussing the validity of various death tolls linked to Mongol expansion, such as 1,000,000 people in Nishapur and 60 million people in China, and using primary sources and historians' interpretations

describing the contrasting perspectives on the Fall of Constantinople (1453), including prophecies and legends, and how these shaped historians' interpretations of the experiences of people living at the time
analysing the extent to which historians' interpretations are corroborated with the oral histories contained in Icelandic sagas, such as about Erik the Red founding Greenland
The Spanish conquest of the Americas
analysing the extent to which historians' interpretations that the Spanish conquest can be attributed to the pursuit of "Gold, God and Glory" differ

nodes.label: Sources, evidence and interpretive uncertainty
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the nature and availability of sources shapes the interpretations historians can make about the chosen empire or expansion — including how different source types produce different perspectives.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand how source availability and type shape interpretation cannot critically evaluate competing historical accounts. The source-interpretation link is prerequisite to all interpretive analysis.
criteria: Explains how at least one source type shapes the interpretations historians can make about the chosen empire
Identifies at least one limitation of the available sources and explains how it affects historical understanding

width.minimum: An explanation of how at least one source type (e.g. oral tradition, primary chronicle, archaeological record) shapes interpretations of the chosen empire.
width.typical: The relationship between source type and interpretive possibility across the chosen empire. Examples: Icelandic sagas as oral histories corroborated or contested by archaeological evidence (Erik the Red's Greenland settlements, L'Anse aux Meadows); how the written accounts of monks shaped Viking historiography; the validity of various death tolls linked to Mongol expansion and how these are evaluated against primary and secondary sources.
wider: Analyse the extent to which historians' interpretations are corroborated with oral histories in Icelandic sagas — examining where archaeological and saga accounts align and where they diverge — as a case study in how oral and written sources produce different historical pictures

Examine why death toll estimates linked to Mongol expansion (e.g. 1,000,000 in Nishapur, 60 million in China) are contested, and how historians evaluate such claims using primary sources and demographic reasoning

modes.reason: Students often treat historical sources as simply reliable or unreliable. Scaffold the more nuanced idea: different source types (oral, written, archaeological) produce different kinds of evidence that historians must weigh against each other. This is more complex than a simple accuracy check.

nodes.label: Competing interpretations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe competing historical interpretations of the chosen empire or expansion and explain why they differ — including how the perspective of the interpreter, access to sources, and historical context shape the conclusions reached.
criteria: Describes at least two competing historical interpretations of the chosen empire or expansion
Explains at least one reason why the interpretations differ, with reference to evidence, perspective or historical context

width.minimum: Two different interpretations of the chosen empire or expansion with at least one explanation of why they differ.
width.typical: Multiple competing interpretations with analysis of their bases. Examples: contrasting perspectives on the Fall of Constantinople (1453) — prophecies and legends vs historical analysis; the 'Gold, God and Glory' framework for Spanish conquest and how it is contested; differing interpretations of Viking raids vs Viking trade and settlement.
wider: Examine contrasting perspectives on the Fall of Constantinople (1453) — including prophecies, legends and historians' accounts — and analyse how these shaped understanding of the experiences of people living at the time

Analyse the extent to which the 'Gold, God and Glory' interpretation of the Spanish conquest holds — examining how different historians weight religious, economic and political motivations and what evidence each draws on

modes.reason: The range of interpretive contests across different empires is wide — Mongol death tolls, Viking reputation, Fall of Constantinople, Spanish conquest. Using more than one example of interpretive contest prevents students from treating historical debate as specific to one case.

nodes.label: Evaluating interpretations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate competing interpretations of the chosen empire or expansion — identifying which is better supported by evidence and explaining the reasoning behind that judgement.
criteria: Evaluates at least one historical interpretation of the chosen empire or expansion using evidence
Explains why the interpretation is well-supported or limited, with reference to specific sources or reasoning

width.minimum: An evaluation of at least one interpretation using evidence to assess its strengths or limitations.
width.typical: Evaluation of competing interpretations using source evidence; how the perspective of subject peoples vs rulers produces different interpretive frameworks; the role of archaeological evidence in confirming or revising written-source interpretations (e.g. Viking settlements at L'Anse aux Meadows vs saga accounts).
wider: Evaluate the 'Gold, God and Glory' framework against primary source evidence of conquistador motivations, identifying where the interpretation is well-supported, where it oversimplifies, and what it leaves out

Examine how post-colonial perspectives on the Spanish conquest have changed historical interpretations — particularly around the experiences of Indigenous peoples — and evaluate how this represents an improvement in historical understanding

modes.reason: Evaluation integrates source analysis (Node 1) and competing interpretation identification (Node 2). Invest in helping students move from noting that interpretations differ to making a reasoned judgement about which is better supported — this is the full demand of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Features of Asia-Pacific society
descriptors.description: the significant social, religious, cultural, economic, environmental and/or political features of different groups in the Asian-Pacific society
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain the significant social, religious, cultural, economic and political features of ancient and early societies (AC9HH7K09–K11). They understand how to describe a society across multiple dimensions. They have not yet examined these features in Asia-Pacific contexts — the Khmer Empire, feudal Japan under the Shoguns, or Polynesian societies including Māori and Rapa Nui.
elaborations: describing the way of life in the Khmer Empire as depicted through stone carvings and the writings of the Chinese Ambassador Zhou Daguan; for example, in relation to fishing, trading in markets, temple construction
Japan under the Shoguns

describing the way of life in feudal Japan under the shoguns; for example, "bushido" – the chivalric code of conduct of the samurai that emphasised frugality, loyalty, mastery of martial arts and honour
analysing how the relationship between the different social classes, such as the emperor, shogun, daimyo, samurai and workers, promoted social and cultural continuity
Polynesian expansion across the Pacific
describing the way of life in one Polynesian society, including the social, cultural, economic and political features, such as the role of the ariki in Māori and in Rapa Nui society

investigating the way of life of Easter Island (Rapa Nui) society; for example, fishing by the men; links between the household and the extended clan through the exchange of goods, wives and labour; the use of stone tools

nodes.label: Social and political organisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the social and political organisation of the chosen Asia-Pacific society — including the roles of different social classes, the distribution of political authority, and how social hierarchies structured daily life.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the social and political hierarchy of the chosen society is prerequisite to analysing how turning points disrupted it, how power was exercised within it, and what significant individuals achieved against this backdrop. The social structure is the frame for all subsequent analysis.
criteria: Names the main social groups in the chosen society and describes their roles and relationships
Explains how the social hierarchy organised access to power, resources or status

width.minimum: A description of the social hierarchy of the chosen society with at least two groups and their roles.
width.typical: The social and political hierarchy across the chosen society. Examples: the Khmer Empire as depicted through stone carvings and Zhou Daguan's writings — fishing, trading, temple construction; feudal Japan under the shoguns — emperor, shogun, daimyo, samurai, workers — and how these classes promoted social and cultural continuity; Polynesian social organisation including the role of the ariki in Māori and Rapa Nui society; Rapa Nui clan structure — the household and extended clan linked through exchange of goods, wives and labour.
wider: For feudal Japan: analyse how the relationship between different social classes — emperor, shogun, daimyo, samurai and workers — promoted social and cultural continuity, examining why the hierarchy was stable over long periods
For Polynesian societies: compare the role of the ariki (chief) in Māori and Rapa Nui societies to examine how similar social structures produced different cultural practices across the Pacific

modes.reason: Students often describe social hierarchies as a list of roles without explaining how they are held together — what obligations, dependencies and belief systems maintain the structure. Scaffold the relational logic of the hierarchy.

nodes.label: Religious and cultural practices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the religious beliefs and cultural practices of the chosen Asia-Pacific society and explain how these shaped social order, cultural identity and political authority.
criteria: Describes at least one religious or cultural practice of the chosen society with historically specific detail
Explains the social or political function of that practice — what it sustained or organised within the society

width.minimum: A description of at least one religious or cultural practice and its social or political function.
width.typical: Religious and cultural features in relation to their social function. Examples: bushido — the samurai code of conduct emphasising frugality, loyalty, martial arts mastery and honour — as a cultural system sustaining feudal Japan; Khmer temple construction (Angkor Wat) as a demonstration of the god-king's power; Polynesian cultural practices — tapa cloth, navigational knowledge, oral traditions; the role of stone tools and fishing in Rapa Nui society.
wider: For feudal Japan: examine bushido as a cultural system that simultaneously trained individual warriors and maintained systemic loyalty across the feudal hierarchy
For the Khmer Empire: examine the concept of the 'deva-raja' (god-king) as a religious-political fusion that enabled Khmer kings to mobilise the population for both construction and warfare

modes.reason: Religious and cultural practices vary significantly across the three possible Asia-Pacific contexts. Using more than one context (e.g. samurai bushido vs Polynesian ariki traditions vs Khmer god-king ideology) prevents students from generalising from a single case.

nodes.label: Economic and environmental features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the economic activities and environmental context of the chosen Asia-Pacific society and explain how these shaped the way of life of different groups.
criteria: Describes at least one economic activity of the chosen society and explains how it related to the environmental context
Identifies how economic features shaped the roles and experiences of at least one social group

width.minimum: A description of at least one economic activity and its relationship to the social or environmental context.
width.typical: Economic and environmental features across agriculture, trade, resource use and technology. Examples: Khmer fishing, market trading and temple construction labour; the environmental management of feudal Japan — Tokugawa regulations on farming and tree harvesting; Polynesian economic practices — aquaculture in Nauru, agricultural practices in Hawaii, exchange systems in Rapa Nui; Rapa Nui men's fishing and household-clan exchange of goods.
wider: For feudal Japan: examine the Tokugawa Shogunate's attempts to curb deforestation — heavy regulations on farmers, managing tree harvesting, lighter construction techniques — as an example of environmental management as governance

For Polynesian societies: investigate how environmental challenges were overcome on different islands to make settlement possible (aquaculture in Nauru, agriculture in Hawaii) to show how Polynesian societies adapted to diverse Pacific environments

modes.reason: Students need to see the link between economic capacity, environmental context and social organisation — e.g. how Khmer water management enabled the agricultural surplus that supported temple construction and a ruling class. Scaffold this causal chain explicitly.

descriptors.title: Turning points in Asia-Pacific
descriptors.description: a significant development, event, turning point or challenge that contributed to continuity and change in the Asian-Pacific society
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand the concept of turning points and continuity and change from AC9HH8K03. They understand the social, cultural and economic features of the chosen Asia-Pacific society (AC9HH8K12). They have not yet applied turning point analysis to the specific context of Asia-Pacific societies — the decline of the Khmer Empire, changes in Shogunate power, Polynesian expansion, or environmental challenges.
elaborations: investigating theories about the decline of the Khmer Empire; for example, the development of an unstable climate such as drought and monsoons, the rise of Theravada Buddhism, the breakdown of Angkor's water management system

explaining how being revered as the "god-king" or "deva-raja" enabled the Khmer kings to rule over the empire with absolute authority, thereby enhancing their ability to mobilise the population to defend the empire as well as to invade neighbours
explaining the significance of the archaeological site of Angkor Wat as a demonstration of the empire's power
explaining how archaeologists and paleo-environmentalists have established the prevalence of droughts in the 14th–15th centuries and the impact of these droughts on the empire
Japan under the Shoguns
explaining reasons for Japan's closure to foreigners under the Tokugawa Shogunate and the impact of US Commodore Perry's visit in 1853
explaining the continuity of Shogunate power in areas such as trade, resource use and social classes

outlining the reasons for attempts by the Tokugawa Shogunate to curb deforestation, such as imposing heavy regulations on farmers, managing the harvesting of trees, and using new, lighter and more efficient construction techniques
explaining the role of the daimyo in contributing to the end of the Ashikaga Shogunate
Polynesian expansion across the Pacific
outlining different theories about the expansion; for example, west–east and east–west movements of settling peoples, and/or the expansion as accidental versus intentional

investigating the construction of the moai (giant statues) on Easter Island (Rapa Nui), the techniques used to make and transport them, and theories about their meaning, such as that they are representations of dead ancestors or chiefs
explaining the significance of Rahui as a way of prohibiting the collection of resources to ensure their sustainability as a response to the decline and extinction of animals such as the moa
explaining how environmental challenges were overcome on different islands to make settlement possible; for example, the practice of aquaculture in Nauru and/or agricultural practices in Hawaii

nodes.label: The development and its historical context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a significant turning point or challenge in the chosen Asia-Pacific society and explain how it fits within the broader trajectory of that society's development.
criteria: Identifies a specific turning point or challenge in the chosen Asia-Pacific society and situates it in the society's broader history
Distinguishes between the turning point as an event and the longer-term conditions that enabled it

width.minimum: Identification of a specific turning point with an explanation of its place in the society's history.
width.typical: The turning point situated within the chosen society's broader arc. Examples: theories about the decline of the Khmer Empire (climate instability, rise of Theravada Buddhism, breakdown of water management); Japan's closure to foreigners under the Tokugawa Shogunate and the impact of US Commodore Perry's visit (1853); Polynesian expansion — west-east and east-west movement theories, accidental vs intentional settlement; construction of the Rapa Nui moai and theories about their meaning; the role of Rahui in resource conservation.
wider: For the Khmer: examine how archaeologists and paleo-environmentalists have established the prevalence of droughts in the 14th–15th centuries and their impact on the empire, showing how environmental science can contribute to historical understanding

For Polynesia: examine the significance of Rahui — prohibiting collection of resources to ensure sustainability — as a turning point in resource management, connecting Indigenous environmental knowledge to the concept of historical change

modes.reason: Students need to situate the turning point within the society's trajectory before analysing its causes and effects. Scaffold the contextualisation: what was the state of the society before, and in what direction did the turning point shift it?

nodes.label: Causes and features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the causes and key features of the chosen turning point, drawing on primary and secondary sources — including archaeological, environmental and written evidence.
nodes.hinge_reason: A well-evidenced causal account is prerequisite to analysing effects on continuity and change. Students who cannot describe what happened and why cannot explain what it changed.
criteria: Identifies at least two causes of the chosen turning point, distinguishing between immediate triggers and longer-term conditions
Describes key features using at least one source type (archaeological, written or environmental) as evidence

width.minimum: At least two causes and a description of the key features of the turning point, with reference to at least one source.
width.typical: Multiple causes (immediate and longer-term) with detailed description of features. Examples: the Khmer decline — Tai invasions, Jayavarman VII's building program, population growth, religious revolution, environmental challenges, water management failure; the role of the daimyo in ending the Ashikaga Shogunate; Polynesian expansion — construction techniques, wayfinding, moai construction techniques and transport; the decline of the moa and application of Rahui.
wider: For the Khmer: examine the significance of Angkor Wat as a demonstration of imperial power — and how the same resources invested in its construction (labour, materials, administrative capacity) may have contributed to the empire's eventual fragility

For the moai: investigate the construction and transport of moai on Rapa Nui — techniques and theories about their meaning as representations of ancestors or chiefs — as a case study in how monuments can reveal the values and capacities of a society

modes.reason: The causes of major turning points in Asia-Pacific societies are often multi-factor and span environmental, political and cultural domains. Students need sufficient accumulated specific knowledge before they can make well-supported causal claims.

nodes.label: Effects and continuity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the effects of the chosen turning point on the Asia-Pacific society — describing what changed for different groups and what remained the same — and evaluate its historical significance.
criteria: Explains at least one change and one continuity resulting from the turning point, with reference to specific evidence
Identifies how the turning point affected at least one social group and evaluates its historical significance

width.minimum: At least two effects (one change and one continuity) for at least one affected group.
width.typical: Multiple effects across domains for different groups. Examples: Khmer decline effects on different classes; the continuity of Shogunate power in trade, resource use and social classes under the Tokugawa alongside the change represented by Japan's isolation; Polynesian expansion effects — successful settlement of diverse Pacific island environments; the significance of different theories of expansion (accidental vs intentional) for how we understand Pacific peoples' capabilities.
wider: For feudal Japan: explain the reasons for Japan's closure to foreigners under the Tokugawa Shogunate and the impact of US Commodore Perry's visit (1853) as a turning point — examining both the continuities maintained by isolation and the rapid change it ultimately failed to prevent

For Polynesian expansion: outline different theories (west-east vs east-west, accidental vs intentional) and evaluate which is better supported by archaeological and environmental evidence, examining how theories about expansion affect how we understand Polynesian identity and capability

modes.reason: Asia-Pacific turning points span environmental, political, military and cultural domains. Using multiple domains — and noting what continued as well as what changed — builds a more complete analysis of historical significance.

descriptors.title: Power and authority in Asia-Pacific
descriptors.description: the experiences and perspectives of rulers and of subject peoples, and the interaction between power and/or authority in the Asian-Pacific society
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how power and authority operated in medieval European and imperial contexts (AC9HH8K04, AC9HH8K09) and the social hierarchy of the chosen Asia-Pacific society (AC9HH8K12). They have not yet analysed how power and authority specifically operated in Asia-Pacific contexts — including the Khmer god-king, the Tokugawa feudal system, or chiefly authority in Polynesian societies.
elaborations: analysing the perspectives of Angkor as depicted through stone carvings and the writings of Chinese Ambassador Zhou Daguan; for example, in relation to fishing, trading in markets and temple construction
Japan under the Shoguns
discussing the role of the Tokugawa Shogunate in reimposing a feudal system (based on daimyo and samurai) and explaining the impact of this change on the daily life of different classes
Polynesian expansion across the Pacific
examining artefacts such as Lapita pottery from Vanuatu, tapa cloth and/or ship-building techniques to provide insight into those societies
describing the responsibilities and privileges of being a chief in a society such as those in New Zealand, Hawaii, Tonga and/or the Society Islands

nodes.label: How rulers exercised authority
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how rulers in the chosen Asia-Pacific society exercised authority — including the basis of their legitimacy, the mechanisms of their rule, and how they mobilised or controlled subject peoples.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how rulers exercised and legitimised authority is prerequisite to understanding how subject peoples experienced and responded to it. Students who cannot explain the basis of rulers' power cannot analyse the perspectives of those subject to it.
criteria: Identifies at least two mechanisms through which rulers in the chosen society exercised authority
Explains the basis of the ruler's legitimacy — what gave them the right to rule in the eyes of their subjects

width.minimum: At least two mechanisms through which rulers exercised authority, with reference to the basis of their legitimacy.
width.typical: The mechanisms and legitimacy of rule across the chosen society. Examples: the Khmer deva-raja (god-king) enabling absolute authority through religious legitimacy — mobilising the population for defence and construction; the Tokugawa Shogunate reimposing a feudal system based on daimyo and samurai and its impact on daily life across classes; the responsibilities and privileges of chiefs (ariki) in Polynesian societies such as New Zealand, Hawaii, Tonga and the Society Islands.
wider: For the Khmer: analyse the perspectives of Angkor as depicted through stone carvings and Zhou Daguan's writings — in relation to fishing, trading and temple construction — as evidence of how royal authority shaped the lives of ordinary people

For Polynesian societies: compare the responsibilities and privileges of being a chief across different societies (Māori, Hawaiian, Tongan) to examine how chiefly authority varied in its form and functions across the Pacific

modes.reason: Students often focus on what rulers did without analysing why subjects accepted or submitted to their authority. Scaffold the distinction between coercive power (force) and legitimate authority (religious, hereditary, customary) and how different societies relied on different combinations.

nodes.label: Experiences of subject peoples
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the experiences and perspectives of subject peoples in the chosen Asia-Pacific society — including how social position, class and cultural context shaped their daily life under authority.
criteria: Describes how authority shaped the daily life of at least one subject group in the chosen Asia-Pacific society
Identifies at least one way in which different groups within the same society experienced authority differently

width.minimum: A description of how authority affected the daily life of at least one subject group.
width.typical: The varied experiences of subject peoples. Examples: the impact of the Tokugawa Shogunate reimposing a feudal system on different classes (daimyo, samurai, farmers, merchants); the use of artefacts such as Lapita pottery from Vanuatu, tapa cloth and ship-building techniques to provide insight into the lives of ordinary Polynesian peoples; how daily life in the Khmer Empire was shaped by the obligations of subject peoples to the god-king.
wider: For feudal Japan: examine the impact of the Tokugawa Shogunate's reimposition of the feudal system on different classes — particularly the impact on merchants and artisans whose wealth grew but whose status remained formally low
For Polynesia: examine artefacts such as Lapita pottery, tapa cloth and ship-building techniques as evidence of the daily life and capabilities of ordinary Polynesian peoples, not just their rulers

modes.reason: The experience of subject peoples under authority varies dramatically across Asia-Pacific societies. Using multiple contexts (Khmer peasants vs Polynesian commoners vs Japanese samurai) prevents students from generalising from a single subordinate experience.

nodes.label: Interactions and responses to authority
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how subject peoples responded to authority in the chosen Asia-Pacific society — including accommodation, resistance or cultural negotiation — and explain how these interactions shaped the society.
criteria: Identifies at least one example of how subject peoples responded to authority in the chosen society
Explains how that response shaped the society — whether maintaining, modifying or challenging existing power structures

width.minimum: At least one example of how subject peoples responded to authority, with an explanation of its effect on the society.
width.typical: Responses across accommodation, resistance and exchange. Examples: how the daimyo contributed to the end of the Ashikaga Shogunate as subject-rulers challenging authority from within; the role of merchants and artisans in feudal Japan navigating formal status constraints; Polynesian peoples' practical sovereignty over resources through Rahui as a community-led response to environmental pressure; the role of councils and collective decision-making in chiefly societies.
wider: For feudal Japan: examine the role of the daimyo in contributing to the end of the Ashikaga Shogunate as a case study in how powerful subject-rulers could challenge and ultimately transform the authority structure from within

For the Khmer: examine how the god-king's authority was both sustained and undermined by his obligation to deliver prosperity — when environmental failure (drought, flooding) disrupted the water management system, the basis of royal authority was challenged

modes.reason: This node integrates understanding of how authority was exercised (Node 1) and experienced (Node 2) into an analysis of how the relationship between rulers and subjects was dynamic rather than fixed. Invest in helping students see authority as a relationship that required ongoing maintenance and negotiation.

descriptors.title: Significant individuals in Asia-Pacific
descriptors.description: the role and achievements of a significant individual and/or group in the Asian-Pacific society
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain the role and achievements of significant individuals in ancient and imperial contexts (AC9HH7K13, AC9HH8K05, AC9HH8K10). They understand the social and cultural features of the chosen Asia-Pacific society (AC9HH8K12). They have not yet applied significance analysis to individuals specifically connected to Asia-Pacific societies — Khmer rulers, Japanese shoguns, or Polynesian groups.
elaborations: describing the rule of Jayavarman VII and his influence in expanding the empire, expelling the Chams and on the scale of the construction program in Angkor
Japan under the Shoguns
explaining the legacy of Tokugawa Ieyasu as founder of the Edo Shogunate
Polynesian expansion across the Pacific
describing the achievements of one Polynesian group of people such as Māori, Samoan, Tahitian (Maohi), Tongans or Rapa Nui

nodes.label: Role and context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the role of the chosen individual or group in their Asia-Pacific society and explain the conditions that enabled their significance.
criteria: Describes the role of the chosen individual or group in their Asia-Pacific society
Identifies at least one condition that enabled their significance

width.minimum: A description of the chosen individual or group's role with reference to the historical conditions that enabled it.
width.typical: The chosen individual or group situated within their society's context. Examples: Jayavarman VII — his rule, expansion of the Khmer Empire, expulsion of the Chams, and the scale of the Angkor construction program; Tokugawa Ieyasu as founder of the Edo Shogunate — the conditions that enabled his consolidation of power; Polynesian groups (Māori, Samoan, Tahitian, Tongan, Rapa Nui) and their achievements in settlement, navigation and cultural development.
wider: For the Khmer: examine Jayavarman VII's rule as both military leader (expelling the Chams) and builder (Angkor's construction program) — and consider whether these two roles were connected or in tension

For Polynesia: compare the achievements of different Polynesian groups across navigation, settlement and cultural development to understand how similar social structures and technologies enabled diverse achievements across the Pacific

modes.reason: Students need to contextualise the individual or group's role before assessing their achievements. Scaffold the question: what conditions made this person's or group's actions possible, and why were they positioned to act as they did?

nodes.label: Achievements and impact
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the key achievements of the chosen individual or group and describe their impact on the society and on later developments.
nodes.hinge_reason: Achievement analysis is the core demand of this descriptor. Students who narrate events rather than explaining achievements and impacts have not met the standard. Legacy analysis depends on solid achievement analysis here.
criteria: Identifies at least two achievements of the chosen individual or group
Explains the impact of at least one achievement on the society and on later developments

width.minimum: At least two achievements with an explanation of their impact on the society.
width.typical: Multiple achievements analysed for immediate and longer-term impact. Examples: Jayavarman VII's expansion of the Khmer Empire and construction program; the legacy of Tokugawa Ieyasu in establishing the Edo Shogunate and Japan's subsequent isolation; the achievements of Polynesian peoples in navigation, settlement of diverse island environments, development of distinctive cultures and resource management practices.
wider: For the Khmer: examine the influence of Jayavarman VII's building program on both the empire's power and its later fragility — asking whether great achievement can also contain the seeds of decline

For Polynesia: describe the achievements of one Polynesian group — their navigation techniques, settlement strategies, cultural innovations — and evaluate what these achievements reveal about the capabilities and values of Pacific peoples

modes.reason: Students often describe what a ruler did without connecting it to impact. Scaffold the distinction: an achievement is not an event but a consequential act. Each achievement needs an explanation of what it changed or enabled for the society.

nodes.label: Legacy and significance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the legacy of the chosen individual or group — explaining what endured from their achievements and how historians or cultural traditions have assessed their significance.
criteria: Explains at least one lasting legacy of the chosen individual or group
Connects the legacy to the society's longer-term history or to contemporary significance

width.minimum: An explanation of at least one lasting legacy and a reference to how the individual or group is regarded in historical or cultural memory.
width.typical: Legacy evaluated across multiple criteria; connections to subsequent historical developments; the relationship between historical judgement and cultural memory. Examples: Tokugawa Ieyasu's legacy in shaping Japan's political culture and later modernisation; the enduring cultural achievements of Polynesian peoples including navigational knowledge, oral traditions and material culture; the architectural legacy of Angkor Wat as a UNESCO World Heritage site.
