width.minimum: Students describe at least two specific changes to women's roles during the war (e.g. entry into previously male workplaces, nursing roles, voluntary organisations) and note whether these changes persisted after the war ended.
width.typical: Students examine the specific roles women took on in paid work (manufacturing, transport, office work), in the voluntary sector (Red Cross, comfort funds, war savings), and as nurses in military hospitals; compare these to women's roles and employment patterns before 1914; examine what happened when men returned — which changes persisted, which reversed; consider what the experience of wartime work meant for women's expectations about employment and rights; connect to the broader suffrage context from AC9HH9K04 and K05.
wider: Examine primary sources from Australian women during the war — letters, diary entries, newspaper reports of women workers — to ground the general pattern in individual voices and perspectives

Investigate how white feather campaigns created social pressure on men to enlist — examining how women were recruited as instruments of conscription pressure even without formal enlistment — and what this reveals about gender and patriotism

modes.reason: Students commonly frame women's wartime roles as simple liberation — 'women got to work' — without examining the complexity of change and continuity, or the coercive aspects of women's wartime participation (white feather campaigns). Multiple examples across different domains of activity prevent oversimplification.

nodes.label: The conscription debates — political crisis and social division
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the two conscription referenda, identify the main groups who supported and opposed conscription and their reasons, and explain why the conscription issue divided Australian society and the Labor Party.
nodes.hinge_reason: The conscription debates are both the most complex political content in this descriptor and the gateway to understanding changes in Australia's relationship with Britain (N4). Students who cannot explain why conscription divided Australia — specifically, who opposed it and why — cannot understand the fracture in the Labor movement, the emergence of new political alignments, or the shift in Australia's sense of independent identity relative to Empire.
criteria: Describes the two conscription referenda, their outcomes, and the role of Billy Hughes
Identifies at least two distinct groups opposing conscription and explains their different grounds for opposition

width.minimum: Students describe that two referenda on conscription were held (1916, 1917), both defeated, identify at least two groups opposing conscription and their main reasons, and explain what role Billy Hughes played.
width.typical: Students explain the military context that prompted conscription proposals — mounting casualties, declining voluntary enlistment; the specific arguments for conscription (military necessity, fairness to those already serving) and against (personal liberty, working-class opposition to an imperialist war, Irish Catholic opposition); the role of Archbishop Daniel Mannix; the split within the Labor Party — Hughes expelled, forming a new government; the role of propaganda for and against in the campaigns; explain why both referenda failed and what this revealed about Australian attitudes to the war and to Britain.
wider: Examine specific referendum campaign materials — 'Vote Yes' and 'Vote No' posters, pamphlets, Hughes' speeches, Mannix's sermons — analysing the rhetorical strategies and emotional appeals on each side

Compare Australia's conscription debates with those in Britain and Canada — why did Australia hold referenda rather than simply legislate, and what does this difference reveal about Australian political culture?

modes.reason: Students commonly treat conscription opposition as simple anti-war sentiment without understanding the multiple distinct bases for opposition — class-based, religious, ethnic, libertarian. Making the distinct grounds for opposition explicit prevents conflation and enables the evaluation of which groups mattered most to the outcome.

Examining sources from both the 'Yes' and 'No' campaigns — and from different types of opponents (trade unionists, Irish Catholics, women's groups, civil libertarians) — builds the picture of social division that the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Australia's changing relationship with Britain
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine the continuities and changes in Australia's relationship with the British Empire as a result of the war, including how the war both affirmed and strained the imperial relationship.
criteria: Describes at least one continuity and one change in Australia's relationship with Britain as a result of the war
Explains how the shared sacrifice at Gallipoli contributed to both a sense of imperial belonging and a distinct Australian national identity

width.minimum: Students describe at least one way the war reinforced Australia's relationship with Britain (fighting together, shared sacrifice) and at least one way it created new tensions or a new sense of distinct Australian identity (Gallipoli as an Australian story, resentment of British command decisions).
width.typical: Students examine the affirmation of Empire loyalty through shared sacrifice; the simultaneous development of a distinctly Australian national identity through the Gallipoli experience (ANZAC as a specifically Australian story); the resentment of British command decisions (Fromelles, Gallipoli) and what this meant for how Australians saw British leadership; the new sense of Australia as a distinct nation that had 'earned its place' on the world stage through sacrifice; the seeds of eventual greater independence in foreign policy.
wider: Examine how Australian and British official histories of the war — Bean's Official History vs British accounts — differ in emphasis and what this reveals about the distinct national narratives being constructed
Trace the trajectory from 1914 Empire loyalty to the growing independence visible in the 1930s and 1940s — connecting this descriptor to longer-term changes in Australian sovereignty

modes.reason: Students commonly frame the relationship with Britain as either straightforwardly loyal or straightforwardly resentful. The content requires holding both — the war both affirmed and complicated the relationship — which requires explicit modelling of how continuity and change can coexist in the same relationship.

nodes.label: Returned soldiers — physical, psychological and social experiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the effects of war on returned soldiers — including physical and psychological trauma, reintegration challenges, social and racial discrimination, and the policy responses — including the experiences of First Nations Australian soldiers.
criteria: Describes at least three distinct types of effects experienced by returned soldiers
Explains the specific additional challenges faced by First Nations Australian returned soldiers, including racial discrimination and unequal access to repatriation benefits

width.minimum: Students describe at least three distinct types of effects on returned soldiers (e.g. physical wounds/disability, shell shock/psychological trauma, employment difficulties) and describe one policy response (e.g. Soldier Settlement Scheme, pensions).
width.typical: Students describe the scale and nature of physical casualties (wounded, disabled, disfigured); explain shell shock as a documented psychological consequence — what symptoms were observed, how it was understood and often dismissed at the time; examine employment reintegration challenges — many returned to a labour market that had changed; the Soldier Settlement Scheme — land allocation to returned soldiers, why many schemes failed; pension access and disputes; the experience of returned soldiers seeking social recognition of their service; apply these patterns specifically to First Nations Australian soldiers' experiences of additional racial discrimination, wage inequality, and exclusion from some repatriation benefits.
wider: Examine personal accounts from returned soldiers — diaries, letters, oral histories — to ground the general patterns in specific human experiences, applying source analysis skills

Investigate the experience of a specific First Nations returned soldier — service record, post-war life, obstacles faced — to make concrete the additional layer of discrimination documented in elaboration 4

modes.reason: Students commonly reduce the returned soldier experience to either heroic recognition or simple suffering. The full range — physical, psychological, economic, social, racial — produces a more complete picture that the descriptor requires.
Individual case studies — including First Nations soldiers — build the accumulated picture of returned soldier experience that allows the pattern to be understood as systemic, not exceptional.

descriptors.title: Commemoration, Anzac legend and historical interpretations
descriptors.description: the commemoration of the First World War, including different historical interpretations and debates about the nature and significance of the Anzac legend and the war
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify that historical interpretations differ and explain why (AC9HH8K06, AC9HH8K11). They have studied the Gallipoli campaign, the Western Front experience, and the effects of the war on Australian society (AC9HH9K09, AC9HH9K11). They have not yet examined what the 'Anzac legend' claims as a set of values and ideals, how commemoration functions as a cultural practice, or how historians have debated and contested the legend's nature and significance over time.
elaborations: investigating the ideals associated with the Anzac tradition and how and why the First World War is commemorated within Australian society
discussing the similarities and differences in historians' views of the Anzac legend over time
identifying differences between commemoration and glorification of war
evaluating the fairness of post-war treaties on the defeated powers, such as the Treaty of Versailles on Germany

nodes.label: The Anzac legend — what it claims and what values it asserts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the Anzac legend as a set of specific values and ideals — mateship, courage, larrikinism, egalitarianism, endurance — and explain where these ideals came from and what they claim about Australian national character.
nodes.hinge_reason: The Anzac legend's content must be understood before its historiographical debate (N3) can proceed. Students who cannot describe what the legend actually claims cannot meaningfully compare historians' views about its nature and significance — they will discuss the debate without knowing what is being debated.
criteria: Describes the core ideals of the Anzac legend with at least three examples
Explains where the legend came from and what it claims about Australian national character

width.minimum: Students identify the core ideals associated with the Anzac legend (mateship, courage, endurance under adversity, egalitarian disregard for rank, larrikinism), describe where each ideal came from — the Gallipoli and Western Front experience as interpreted by C.E.W. Bean and others — and explain what the legend claims about what it means to be Australian.
width.typical: Students describe the Anzac legend's specific components; trace the legend's origins in C.E.W. Bean's reporting and official histories; explain how the legend was constructed from selective elements of the actual experience (not all soldiers displayed these virtues; the legend emphasises some experiences and omits others); explain what purposes the legend served — national identity, meaning-making for grief, connection to a founding national story; examine how the legend positions Gallipoli as the 'birth' of the Australian nation.
wider: Examine specific texts that constructed the legend — Bean's dispatches, early ANZAC Day speeches, war poetry and art — and analyse the choices made in how soldiers and their experience were represented
Investigate who was excluded from the original legend — First Nations soldiers, women, non-Anglo Australians — and what that exclusion reveals about whose story the legend was originally telling

modes.reason: Students commonly treat the Anzac legend as self-evidently true — the actual soldiers were exactly as described — rather than as a specific historical construction that emphasised some elements and omitted others. Making the legend's constructedness explicit is the scaffold for the interpretive debate that follows.

Examining how the legend was constructed from specific sources — Bean's journalism, specific speeches, specific images — and what each source emphasised, builds a more complex understanding than treating the legend as a single, unified thing.

nodes.label: Commemoration — how and why WW1 is remembered
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how the First World War is commemorated in Australian society and explain the purposes that commemoration serves — including the distinction between commemoration and glorification.
criteria: Describes the main forms of WW1 commemoration in Australia
Distinguishes commemoration from glorification with a clear explanation of what makes each different

width.minimum: Students describe the main forms of WW1 commemoration in Australia (ANZAC Day, memorials, the Last Post, the minute of silence, Dawn Services), explain at least two purposes commemoration serves (honouring the dead, maintaining national memory, community gathering, educating future generations), and identify the distinction between commemorating sacrifice and glorifying war.
width.typical: Students describe the evolution of ANZAC Day from a solemn memorial day to a major national event — changes in scale, participation, and meaning over time; examine the different ways commemoration is practiced (Dawn Services, school ceremonies, sporting tributes, pilgrimages to Gallipoli); explain who participates and why; examine the distinction between commemoration as respectful remembrance of sacrifice vs glorification as celebrating war as heroic and desirable; explain why this distinction matters to those who design commemorative practices.
wider: Compare Australian commemoration practices with those in Turkey, New Zealand, and France — what does each country's approach reveal about how they understand their relationship to WW1?

Investigate how ANZAC Day changed between its founding (1916) and the present — examining periods when participation declined (1950s–60s) and when it resurged (1990s–present) — and what drove each change

modes.reason: Students commonly treat commemoration and glorification as synonymous. Making the distinction explicit — commemoration can honour sacrifice without celebrating war — is both a required endpoint outcome and conceptually important for the historiographical debate node that follows.

nodes.label: Historiographical debate — how historians' views of the Anzac legend have differed over time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss similarities and differences in historians' views of the Anzac legend over time, identifying key interpretive positions and explaining what grounds the debate.
criteria: Identifies at least two different historical interpretations of the Anzac legend and describes what each claims
Explains on what grounds historians hold different views — not just that they disagree, but why their interpretations differ

width.minimum: Students identify at least two distinct historical interpretations of the Anzac legend — e.g. the traditional celebratory view, revisionist critiques (that the legend is a myth, that it glorifies war, that it excludes women and non-Anglo Australians), and more recent inclusive expansions — and explain on what grounds historians hold different views.
width.typical: Students describe the traditional legend (Bean, early official histories); the revisionist critiques from the 1970s–90s (questions about whether the legend was 'true', whether it glorified war, gender and racial exclusions); responses to revisionism (defending the legend's essential truth while acknowledging limitations); recent expansions to include First Nations soldiers, women, and multicultural contributions; explain what has changed in historians' views and what has driven the changes (new sources, new social values, new questions); explain that historians' disagreements reflect not just different evidence but different values about what the past should mean for the present.
wider: Read extracts from contrasting historians — e.g. Alistair Thomson's 'Anzac Memories', Peter Stanley's work on the legend's exclusions, or a traditional defence of the legend — and compare their claims directly, applying source analysis skills

Consider the question: is the Anzac legend a harmless national story, a positive source of values, or a dangerous myth? Develop a position and support it with historical evidence — this is an evaluative task grounded in the historiographical debate

modes.reason: Students commonly treat 'historians disagree' as meaning 'nobody knows' rather than 'different evidence and different values produce different interpretations'. Making explicit what grounds a valid historical interpretation — evidence, methodology, context, values — is the scaffold for this node.

Encountering multiple distinct interpretive positions — traditional, revisionist, inclusive, evaluative — prevents students from collapsing the debate to a binary 'true or false' question about the legend.

nodes.label: The Treaty of Versailles — fairness and consequences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the fairness of the Treaty of Versailles on Germany, identifying its main terms and assessing the grounds on which it can be considered just or unjust.
criteria: Identifies the main terms of the Treaty of Versailles and describes the German reaction
Evaluates the fairness of the treaty using at least two different perspectives and supports the judgement with evidence

width.minimum: Students identify the main terms imposed on Germany by the Treaty of Versailles (war guilt clause, reparations, territorial losses, military restrictions), describe the German reaction to the treaty, and make a judgement about whether the treaty was fair, supported by at least one reason.
width.typical: Students describe the 'Big Three' negotiating positions (Wilson's Fourteen Points, Clemenceau's punitive aims, Lloyd George's middle position); the specific terms imposed; the German delegation's exclusion from negotiations and their response (the 'diktat'); the war guilt clause (Article 231) as both legally and morally contested; the scale of reparations and territorial loss; evaluate the treaty using multiple criteria — the Allied perspective (Germany started the war and must pay), the German perspective (the terms were unprecedented and punitive), and a longer-term perspective (did the treaty's severity contribute to the conditions for WW2?); connect to the 'stab-in-the-back' myth from AC9HH9K10.
wider: Compare the Treaty of Versailles with Wilson's Fourteen Points — how much of Wilson's vision was actually implemented, and why did the final treaty diverge from it?

Evaluate the claim that the Treaty of Versailles caused WW2 — is this a defensible historical interpretation or an oversimplification? Apply the concept of turning point from AC9HH9K10 to this question

modes.reason: Students commonly judge the Treaty of Versailles as 'unfair' without engaging with the Allied perspective on why it was constructed as it was. Evaluating fairness requires holding multiple perspectives simultaneously — what counts as fair from each party's position — before reaching a reasoned judgement.
Examining the treaty from German, Allied, and longer-term historical perspectives builds the multiperspective understanding the evaluation task requires.

descriptors.title: Causes and effects of the industrial revolution
descriptors.description: the social, economic, political, technological and/or environmental causes and effects of the Industrial Revolution on Europe in the late 18th and 19th century
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe significant developments and their causes and effects in earlier periods (AC9HH8K03, AC9HH8K07). They have not yet examined the Industrial Revolution as a multi-causal, multi-domain transformation — the specific role of technology, the Agricultural Revolution preconditions, the spread of industrialisation across Europe, or how to evaluate the relative significance of multiple causes.
elaborations: explaining how changes in technology, such as steam-driven spinning mills, railways and steam ships, led to the development of factories and industrialised cities
identifying the spread of innovations such as steam power, iron and steel production, transport and the use of new chemicals in Europe, the USA and Japan
analysing factors that caused the Industrial Revolution
evaluating the most significant effects of the Industrial Revolution

nodes.label: Preconditions for industrialisation — why Britain first
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the preconditions that enabled industrialisation to begin in Britain and explain why industrialisation began there rather than elsewhere.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding why industrialisation began in Britain rather than elsewhere is the prerequisite for understanding both the technology node (N2) and the significance evaluation in N4. Students who treat the Industrial Revolution as simply 'machines were invented' cannot explain why it was transformative or how it spread, nor can they engage the multi-causal analysis the descriptor demands.
criteria: Identifies at least three preconditions for industrialisation and explains how each contributed
Explains why industrialisation began in Britain rather than other European nations

width.minimum: Students identify at least three preconditions for industrialisation in Britain (e.g. Agricultural Revolution, access to coal and iron, commercial infrastructure, Enlightenment ideas, imperial trade) and explain how each contributed.
width.typical: Students describe the Agricultural Revolution as releasing labour from the land; access to coal and iron ore as raw material foundations; the existing commercial infrastructure (banks, insurance, joint-stock companies); the legal framework for property rights and patents; Enlightenment ideas about progress and experimentation; the imperial trade network as both a source of capital and a market for manufactured goods; a growing population creating both labour supply and demand; explain why these conditions combined in Britain rather than France, the Netherlands or China.
wider: Evaluate the relative weight of different preconditions — which was most important? Develop a supported argument and anticipate objections

Examine why China, which had many of the technological preconditions, did not industrialise first — exploring what this comparison reveals about the relative importance of social, political and economic conditions vs purely technological ones

modes.reason: Students commonly treat the Industrial Revolution as a story of invention (steam engine → factories) without understanding the social, economic and political preconditions that made invention commercially viable and transformative. Making the preconditions explicit is the scaffold for multi-causal analysis throughout the standard.

nodes.label: Technology and the factory system — steam, iron and textiles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how key technological changes — steam-driven machinery, iron and steel production, railways — led to the development of factories and industrialised cities.
criteria: Describes steam power and at least one other key technology, explaining how each enabled industrial development
Explains the connection between factory growth and the development of industrial cities

width.minimum: Students describe the steam engine as the core technology, explain how it enabled factories and railways, and describe the resulting growth of industrial cities.
width.typical: Students describe the development of steam power (Watt's improvements, stationary engines in factories, mobile engines in railways and ships); the role of iron and steel production in enabling machinery, railways and buildings; the textile industry (spinning jenny, power loom) as the first industrialised factory sector; how railways connected industrial cities and created integrated national markets; how steam power in ships enabled global trade expansion; explain the city-factory connection — factories concentrated workers in urban areas, cities grew to house and supply them.
wider: Examine a specific technological innovation in depth — e.g. the Rocket locomotive (Stephenson, 1829) — and trace its effects across multiple domains (transport, manufacturing, settlement patterns, trade)
Investigate the spread of steam technology beyond Britain to Europe, the USA and Japan — examining how technology transfer happened and what adapted or changed in different national contexts

modes.reason: Students commonly describe the steam engine as important without understanding the mechanism — how it enabled the factory system (replacing human and water power), how railways created integrated markets, how the combination of factory and city growth is causally connected. Making these connections explicit builds the causal picture the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: The spread of industrialisation — Europe, USA and Japan
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how industrialisation spread from Britain to Europe, the USA and Japan, and identify the spread of key innovations (steam power, iron and steel, transport, new chemicals).
criteria: Describes the spread of industrialisation to at least two regions beyond Britain
Identifies at least two innovations that spread with industrialisation and describes how each spread

width.minimum: Students describe industrialisation spreading to at least two other regions (e.g. Europe, USA, Japan) and identify at least two innovations that spread with it.
width.typical: Students describe the spread to continental Europe (Belgium, France, Germany) from the 1820s–50s; the American industrialisation (New England textile mills, railroad expansion, Civil War steel production); the Japanese Meiji Restoration (1868) as a deliberately state-directed industrialisation; the role of technology transfer — deliberate copying, patent breaking, hiring of British engineers; the spread of railways, steel production, chemical industries; explain what was similar and different about industrialisation in different national contexts.
wider: Compare the Japanese Meiji industrialisation with the British model — examining how state-directed industrialisation produced a different social and political outcome to Britain's more market-driven process
Examine how the spread of industrialisation connected to European imperial expansion — the industrial powers had major military and economic advantages that shaped the rest of the 19th century

modes.reason: Students commonly treat industrialisation as a British story without understanding it as a global process of uneven development. Multiple national examples build the comparative picture required by the descriptor.

nodes.label: Effects of the Industrial Revolution — evaluating significance across domains
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the range of effects of the Industrial Revolution — economic, social, political, environmental — and evaluate which effects were most significant.
criteria: Describes effects of the Industrial Revolution across at least three domains
Evaluates which effect was most significant and defends the judgement with evidence

width.minimum: Students describe at least three distinct effects across different domains (e.g. economic growth, changing working conditions, growth of the middle class, environmental impacts) and make a judgement about which was most significant.
width.typical: Students describe effects across all major domains — economic growth and GDP rise; changing social structures (growth of industrial working class and middle class, decline of artisan craft economy); changing working conditions (factory discipline, long hours, child labour, urbanisation); new political ideas (socialism, trade unionism, chartism) emerging in response to industrial conditions; environmental impacts (pollution, deforestation, urban squalor); the rise of imperialism as industrial nations competed for markets and raw materials; evaluate significance — which effect had the greatest long-term consequences — and defend a position with evidence.
wider: Examine the environmental effects of industrialisation in depth — urban pollution, river contamination, coal mining landscapes — and connect to contemporary environmental concerns

Evaluate the 'standard of living debate' — did industrialisation improve or worsen living standards for the majority of British people in the 19th century? Examine the evidence and the historiographical debate

modes.reason: Evaluating significance requires students to draw on knowledge from all domains — economic, social, political, environmental — and synthesise into a supported judgement. This is the full-descriptor integration task.

descriptors.title: Effects of population movements — short, medium and long-term
descriptors.description: the short-, medium- and long-term effects of population movements and changing settlement patterns during this period, such as global demographic changes, transport, new ideas, and political and social reforms
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the movement of peoples and the growth of industrial cities (AC9HH9K014, AC9HH9K13). They have not yet applied a short/medium/long-term temporal framework to evaluate effects, or examined how population movements produced effects across multiple timescales simultaneously.
elaborations: describing the impact of factories, mines and cities on the environment, and on population growth and distribution
investigating the impact of the development of the steam engine on transport, manufacturing and trade
explaining how social and political reforms resulted in higher standards of living for many, including in health care and education, and political and workplace reforms

nodes.label: Short/medium/long-term as an analytical framework
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the short/medium/long-term analytical framework and apply it to distinguish immediate, developing, and lasting effects of a historical process.
nodes.hinge_reason: The analytical framework is the prerequisite for the content nodes. Students who cannot distinguish temporal categories will produce accounts that list effects without organising them — conflating immediate disruptions with lasting structural changes.
criteria: Defines short-, medium- and long-term and explains how each differs
Applies the framework to identify one effect at each timescale for a named historical change

width.minimum: Students define each temporal category and apply the framework to one example — identifying one short-term, one medium-term, and one long-term effect of a named historical change.
width.typical: Students define short-term (immediate, within years), medium-term (developing over decades), and long-term (lasting across generations or centuries) effects; explain that the same historical process can have different effects at different timescales — an effect that seems negative in the short term may be positive long-term, and vice versa; apply the framework to industrial urbanisation as a worked example.
wider: Examine a case where short-term and long-term effects of the same development are in tension — e.g. factory employment was damaging short-term but contributed to long-term wage rises and reform — and evaluate how to weigh these competing effects

modes.reason: Students commonly describe effects without temporal differentiation — treating all effects as equivalent regardless of timescale. Making the framework explicit is the scaffold for the structured analysis the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Environmental and demographic effects of industrialisation and urbanisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the effects of factories, mines and cities on the environment and on population growth and distribution, across short, medium and long timescales.
criteria: Describes at least two environmental effects of industrialisation with temporal classification
Explains how urbanisation changed population distribution and the resulting social conditions

width.minimum: Students describe at least two environmental effects of industrialisation (e.g. urban air pollution, river contamination, mining landscapes) and explain how urbanisation changed population distribution.
width.typical: Students describe the environmental effects — urban air pollution from coal combustion, river and waterway contamination from industrial effluent, the physical transformation of mining landscapes, deforestation for fuel and construction; the demographic effects — rapid urbanisation as rural populations moved to cities, overcrowding and disease in industrial slums, demographic growth driven by industrial demand for labour; apply the temporal framework — immediate pollution effects (short), cumulative disease burden (medium), lasting landscape and demographic shifts (long).
wider: Examine historical data on air quality, river pollution or urban mortality rates to ground the environmental effects in quantitative evidence
Connect the industrial environmental effects to contemporary environmental challenges — examining what continuities exist between 19th-century industrialisation and present-day climate change

modes.reason: Students commonly describe industrialisation's environmental effects as peripheral to the 'real' economic story. Examining environmental effects as primary outcomes — not side-effects — across multiple domains builds the fuller picture the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Transport transformation — the steam engine's effects on movement and trade
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the impact of the development of the steam engine on transport, manufacturing and trade — including the effects of railways and steam shipping on settlement patterns and economic integration.
criteria: Describes the effects of railways and steam shipping on trade and settlement patterns
Explains how transport transformation reduced the friction of distance and its economic consequences

width.minimum: Students describe railways and steam shipping as the two main transport transformations, and explain how each affected trade and settlement patterns.
width.typical: Students describe railway development — connecting industrial cities, enabling movement of goods and people, creating new settlements around junctions, allowing national market integration; steam shipping — enabling faster and more reliable ocean trade, connecting colonial economies to metropolitan centres, enabling larger-scale population movement; explain how transport transformation reduced the friction of distance; how it changed settlement patterns (new towns grew along railways, coastal cities became more important); apply the temporal framework to transport effects.
wider: Examine how railways specifically shaped settlement patterns in Australia (or another settler colonial context) — tracing which towns grew because of railway access and which declined without it
Investigate the role of the Suez Canal (1869) and submarine telegraph cables as transport and communication infrastructure that complemented steam shipping in creating a genuinely globalised economy

modes.reason: Students commonly describe railways as 'faster travel' without understanding the economic and settlement consequences — how reduced transport costs changed what was profitable to produce where, and how railway access determined whether communities grew or stagnated.

nodes.label: Social and political reforms — long-term effects on living standards
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how social and political reforms — in health care, education, political representation, and workplace conditions — resulted in higher standards of living for many over the medium and long term.
criteria: Describes at least two reforms produced by the effects of industrialisation and explains how each improved living standards
Explains the temporal gap between the worst industrial conditions and the reforms that addressed them

width.minimum: Students describe at least two social or political reforms produced by industrialisation's effects (e.g. public health legislation, compulsory education, Factory Acts, trade union recognition) and explain how each improved living standards.
width.typical: Students describe the reform trajectory — from the brutal early industrial period to progressive improvement over the 19th century; specific reforms: Factory Acts limiting child labour and working hours, Public Health Acts addressing urban disease, Education Acts expanding access to schooling, gradual extension of the franchise, trade union recognition; explain how reform came about — the role of evangelical reformers, working-class political pressure, investigative journalism, empirical public health research; apply the temporal framework — reforms were medium and long-term effects of industrialisation, coming decades after the worst conditions.
wider: Examine the role of specific reformers (Florence Nightingale, Edwin Chadwick, Robert Owen) as agents of change — exploring how individuals shaped the reform trajectory
Evaluate who benefited from the reforms and who was left behind — examining whether 'higher standards of living for many' is an accurate characterisation, or whether it conceals persistent inequality

modes.reason: Students commonly treat reform as an inevitable response to bad conditions rather than as a hard-won political achievement. Multiple reform examples across different domains — health, education, labour, political rights — build the fuller picture of gradual improvement through struggle.

descriptors.title: Perspectives and experiences during the industrial revolution
descriptors.description: the different perspectives and experiences of men, women and children during the Industrial Revolution, and their changing way of life
descriptors.knowledge: Students can examine the experiences and perspectives of different groups in historical periods (AC9HH8K04, AC9HH8K09). They have not yet applied this skill to the Industrial Revolution context, examined how technological change affected men, women and children differently, or explored the emergence of trade unions as a collective response to industrial conditions.
elaborations: comparing and contrasting the impact of steam, gas and electricity on people's way of life during the Industrial Revolution
investigating the changes in working conditions, such as longer working hours for low pay and the use of children as a cheap source of labour
identifying the growth of trade unions as a response to the impacts of the Industrial Revolution on the working class

nodes.label: Class differentiation — how industrialisation affected rich and poor differently
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how industrialisation affected people differently depending on their social class, and compare the experiences of the wealthy and the working poor.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that industrialisation produced radically different experiences by class is the prerequisite for understanding the differentiated experiences of men, women and children (N2) and the trade union response (N3). Students who do not have this framework will describe industrialisation as uniformly positive or negative rather than as a process of uneven benefit.
criteria: Describes at least two ways industrialisation improved conditions for wealthy or middle-class people
Describes at least two ways it worsened conditions for the industrial working class

width.minimum: Students describe at least two ways industrialisation improved conditions for wealthy or middle-class people and at least two ways it worsened conditions for the industrial working class.
width.typical: Students describe the benefits for factory owners, merchants and the growing middle class (profit, new goods, consumer products, improved domestic technology); the worsening conditions for industrial workers (factory discipline, long hours, dangerous conditions, low pay, loss of craft autonomy); the new urban poverty — overcrowded slums, disease, polluted water — that contrasted with the prosperity of industrial capitalism; the agricultural worker experience of displacement; explain how the same technological changes produced radically different experiences depending on social position.
wider: Examine the 'two Englands' framing — used by contemporaries including Benjamin Disraeli — as a way of capturing the radical inequality of industrial society
Investigate specific living conditions in an industrial city using census data, social investigations (e.g. Engels' Condition of the Working Class in England) or contemporary journalism

modes.reason: Students commonly describe the Industrial Revolution as either a story of progress (for the wealthy) or suffering (for workers) without understanding how the same process produced both simultaneously. Making the class-differentiated experience explicit is the scaffold for the nuanced perspective analysis the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Gendered and age-based experiences — men, women and children
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the different experiences of men, women and children in industrial workplaces and domestic life, and explain how technological change affected each group's way of life.
criteria: Describes the distinct industrial experience of each of the three groups — men, women and children
Explains how at least one group's experience changed from pre-industrial to industrial conditions

width.minimum: Students describe at least one distinct experience of each group (men, women, children) in the industrial context and explain how it differed from pre-industrial experience.
width.typical: Students describe men's roles in heavy industry, mining, railways — the physical danger, long hours, and how factory discipline transformed working life from craft to machine-paced labour; women's industrial employment — textile mills, domestic service, limited wage levels, the tension between industrial work and domestic responsibilities; children's experiences — as cheap labour in mills, mines and chimneys, the debates about child labour and the Factory Acts; examine how steam, gas and electricity affected domestic life differently for rich and poor households; explain how industrialisation both drew women and children into paid labour and gradually created pressure for their protection from it.
wider: Examine the Parliamentary Select Committee reports and Factory Acts as sources — analysing what the testimony of child workers revealed about conditions and what drove legislative reform

Investigate the contradictions in middle-class attitudes to working-class women and children — the domestic ideal vs economic necessity — and what these contradictions reveal about class and gender values in industrial society

modes.reason: Students commonly focus on one group (often children, as the most dramatic case) without building the full differentiated picture across men, women and children. Multiple examples across all three groups are required.

nodes.label: Trade unions — collective response to industrial conditions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the growth of trade unions as a response to industrialisation's impacts on the working class, and explain what problems trade unions addressed and what they achieved.
criteria: Describes trade unions as a collective response to industrial conditions and explains what problems they addressed
Explains why collective action was necessary when individual workers lacked bargaining power

width.minimum: Students describe trade unions as worker organisations formed to negotiate collectively for wages and conditions, explain what industrial conditions made them necessary, and describe at least one thing they achieved.
width.typical: Students describe the development of trade unions from illegal combinations to recognised organisations; the specific grievances they addressed — long hours, dangerous conditions, child labour, arbitrary dismissal, low wages; early forms of collective action (strikes, mutual aid societies); the legal battles (Combination Acts, their repeal, the Tolpuddle Martyrs); what unions eventually achieved — shorter working hours, improved safety, minimum wage negotiations, political representation through labour parties; explain why collective action was necessary when individual workers had no bargaining power.
wider: Examine the Tolpuddle Martyrs case as a turning point in trade union history — and what it reveals about the balance of power between workers, employers and the state in early industrial Britain
Trace how British trade unionism influenced the Australian labour movement — connecting the Industrial Revolution strand to the Australian Nation strand (AC9HH9K02, K05)

modes.reason: Students commonly treat trade unions as a given feature of industrial society without understanding why collective organisation was necessary — why individual workers had no bargaining power against employers. Making the power asymmetry explicit is the scaffold for understanding why collective action emerged and what it could achieve.

descriptors.title: Ideas that emerged and influenced change
descriptors.description: the ideas that emerged and influenced change in society, such as nationalism, capitalism, imperialism, socialism, egalitarianism and Chartism
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe significant events and their causes and effects (AC9HH8K03, AC9HH8K07). They have not yet examined how abstract political and economic ideas — capitalism, socialism, nationalism, Chartism — emerged from specific historical contexts, or how to explain the basis of an idea and identify the changes it produced.
elaborations: explaining why an idea emerged and the basis of that idea, such as Chartism, and identifying changes that arose from that idea
examining the causes and impacts of the French Revolution on politics and citizens' rights including in the United Kingdom and the USA

examining the role of religious beliefs in the movement to end the slave trade, reforms to improve the negative effects of the Industrial Revolution, the enfranchisement of women and the rise of organised labour

nodes.label: Ideas as historical forces — how ideas emerge from context and produce change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how abstract ideas emerge from specific historical conditions and can identify changes that resulted from them — understanding ideas as historical causes, not just intellectual products.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that ideas have historical contexts and produce historical effects is the conceptual prerequisite for all subsequent nodes. Students who treat ideas as floating intellectual abstractions rather than as historically situated forces cannot explain why specific ideas emerged when they did or why they produced specific changes.
criteria: Explains how at least two ideas emerged from specific historical conditions
Identifies at least one change produced by each idea

width.minimum: Students explain that ideas like capitalism or socialism emerged in response to specific historical conditions (industrialisation, poverty, inequality) and describe at least one change produced by each idea.
width.typical: Students describe capitalism as a systematised defence of private property, free markets and profit — emerging from commercial and industrial expansion; socialism as a critique of capitalism's inequalities — emerging from industrial poverty and exploitation; nationalism as the idea that shared culture/language/ethnicity should be the basis of political community — emerging from the French Revolution and industrialisation's cultural homogenisation; egalitarianism as a challenge to inherited hierarchy — emerging from Enlightenment ideas and colonial social conditions; explain how each idea found expression in specific political movements and reforms.
wider: Examine the intellectual lineages connecting ideas — how did Enlightenment ideas about reason and rights enable both capitalism (Locke, Smith) and socialism (Marx, Owen)? What shared premise did they both build from?
Evaluate which idea had the greatest impact on the modern world — developing a position and anticipating objections

modes.reason: Students commonly describe historical ideas as truths or opinions rather than as historically situated responses to specific conditions. Making the context-idea-effect chain explicit is the scaffold for the whole standard.

nodes.label: Chartism — a case study in popular political ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why Chartism emerged, describe the basis of its demands, and identify the changes that arose from the Chartist movement.
criteria: Describes the People's Charter's main demands and explains why they emerged in the industrial context
Identifies changes that Chartism contributed to, including long-term legacy

width.minimum: Students describe the People's Charter's main demands (universal male suffrage, secret ballot, payment for MPs, equal electoral districts), explain why these demands emerged in the industrial context, and identify at least one long-term change Chartism contributed to.
width.typical: Students describe the political exclusion of the working class from representation in the 1830s; the specific demands of the Charter and the reasoning behind each; the Chartist campaign — petitions, demonstrations, the three petition drives and their rejection; why Chartism declined (emigration of leaders, economic improvement, partial reform); the long-term legacy — most Chartist demands were eventually implemented (secret ballot 1872, universal male suffrage 1918); examine Chartism as an example of working-class political agency in the industrial period.
wider: Compare Chartism with contemporary working-class political movements — trade unionism, socialist parties — examining what Chartism achieved by political means that unions addressed industrially
Examine Chartism's connections to Australia — William Cuffay transported to Tasmania; British Chartists on Victorian goldfields — tracing how radical political ideas travelled with migrants

modes.reason: Students commonly describe Chartism as a failure because its petitions were rejected without understanding the longer-term influence — most of its demands were eventually enacted. Making the short-term/long-term distinction explicit (building on K15's temporal framework) prevents oversimplification.

nodes.label: The French Revolution — causes, impacts and the spread of new political ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine the causes and impacts of the French Revolution on politics and citizens' rights, including its effects in Britain and the USA.
criteria: Describes main causes of the French Revolution and its key political impacts
Explains how the Revolution's ideas affected political thinking in at least one other country

width.minimum: Students describe the main causes of the French Revolution (inequality, Enlightenment ideas, financial crisis, weak monarchy) and identify at least two political impacts (e.g. declaration of rights, spread of republican ideas, Napoleonic reforms).
width.typical: Students describe the social conditions of pre-revolutionary France; the Enlightenment ideas (Rousseau, Voltaire, Locke) that challenged inherited authority; the fiscal crisis and Estates-General; the Revolution's phases — 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man, constitutional monarchy, Republic, Terror, Directory, Napoleon; the Napoleonic Code's legal reforms; how the Revolution spread the ideas of popular sovereignty, equality before the law, and national self-determination; the reaction in Britain (Burke vs Paine) and the USA (enthusiastic reception of republican ideals); the longer-term effects on European political thought and nationalist movements.
wider: Examine the contrast between Burke's conservative critique and Paine's radical defence of the French Revolution — as a case study in how the same events were interpreted through different value frameworks
Trace how the French Revolution's ideas influenced nationalist movements elsewhere — Latin American independence, Italian Risorgimento, 1848 revolutions across Europe

modes.reason: Students commonly focus on the dramatic events of the Revolution (the Terror, executions) without understanding its ideological significance — that it demonstrated popular sovereignty was possible, and its ideas spread beyond France. Multiple examples of impact across different countries build this picture.

nodes.label: Religious belief and social reform — the role of faith in abolition, labour rights and women's rights
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine the role of religious beliefs in the movement to end the slave trade, in reforms improving industrialisation's negative effects, in the enfranchisement of women, and in the rise of organised labour.
criteria: Describes the role of religious belief in at least two reform movements with specific examples
Explains why religious conviction motivated reform — what theological or moral basis underpinned each case

width.minimum: Students describe the role of religious belief in at least two of the four reform areas and explain why religious conviction motivated reform in each case.
width.typical: Students describe the Evangelical and Quaker role in abolition (Wilberforce, the Clapham Sect, the Society of Friends); the role of the Social Gospel movement in labour reform; the role of temperance and Methodist Christianity in women's suffrage campaigns (Christian Women's Temperance Union in Australia); Pope Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum (1891) as a Catholic response to socialism and capitalism defending workers' rights; explain why religious conviction motivated reform — belief in human dignity, equality before God, social responsibility; examine the tension between religious conservatism (defending existing social order) and religious radicalism (challenging inequality in God's name).
wider: Examine how religious reformers and secular radicals sometimes allied and sometimes conflicted in the same reform movements — what did they share and where did they diverge?
Investigate a specific religious reformer in depth — Wilberforce, Florence Nightingale, or Pope Leo XIII — examining how religious conviction shaped their approach and what they achieved

modes.reason: Students commonly treat religious belief and social reform as separate historical domains. Examining how faith motivated specific reform campaigns — not as incidental background but as the driving conviction — builds a more complex understanding of how change happened.

descriptors.title: Significant individuals and groups in promoting ideas
descriptors.description: the role of a significant individual or group such as agricultural and factory workers, inventors and entrepreneurs, landowners, politicians and religious groups in promoting and enacting some of the ideas that emerged during the Industrial Revolution
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the role of significant individuals and groups in historical change (AC9HH8K05, AC9HH8K10, AC9HH8K15) and understand the ideas that emerged during the Industrial Revolution (AC9HH9K17). They have not yet applied the concept of historical agency — the role of individuals in promoting and enacting ideas — to the Industrial Revolution context, or examined how responses to ideas shaped the trajectory of industrial society.
elaborations: explaining responses to particular ideas; for example, how religious groups responded to ideas in Charles Darwin's 1859 book On the Origin of Species or how workers responded to the idea of capitalism or socialism
investigating the role played by an individual or group in promoting a key idea

nodes.label: Historical agency — how individuals and groups promote ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what it means for an individual or group to promote an idea — the distinction between holding an idea and actively working to advance it — and describe the range of strategies available (writing, organising, campaigning, legislating).
nodes.hinge_reason: The agency framework is the prerequisite for the individual/group case studies. Students who cannot distinguish promoting an idea from simply holding it cannot evaluate why specific individuals were significant — what specifically they did that made a difference.
criteria: Explains the distinction between holding an idea and actively promoting it
Identifies at least two strategies for promoting ideas and describes how each works

width.minimum: Students explain that promoting an idea involves active effort to persuade others and enact change, identify at least two strategies for promoting ideas (e.g. writing, public speaking, organising, lobbying), and apply this to one example.
width.typical: Students describe the range of strategies available — publishing (pamphlets, books, newspapers), public speaking and oration, political organisation and campaigning, religious networks, direct action and industrial organisation; explain that the same idea can be promoted by different actors using different strategies; explain that responses to ideas — opposition, revision, partial adoption — are also historically significant forms of agency; connect to the ideas framework from K17.
wider: Compare the effectiveness of different strategies for promoting ideas — when was publishing more effective than organising? When did religious networks reach audiences that secular advocates could not?
Examine how ideas that were initially suppressed or marginalised eventually gained acceptance — what changed to make them viable?

modes.reason: Students commonly describe historical figures as important without articulating what specifically they did to promote an idea. Making the action-mechanism explicit — what did they do, how did they do it, what changed as a result — is the scaffold for meaningful individual investigations.

nodes.label: Responses to ideas — Darwin, capitalism and socialism
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how different groups responded to specific ideas — including how religious groups responded to Darwin's evolutionary theory, and how workers responded to capitalism and socialism.
criteria: Describes at least one group's response to a specific idea, explaining what the response was and why
Explains how values, interests or worldviews shaped how a group received a particular idea

width.minimum: Students describe one case of a group responding to an idea — e.g. religious responses to Darwin, workers embracing socialism — and explain what the response was and why it was made.
width.typical: Students describe Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) and the spectrum of religious responses — outright rejection, theological accommodation, revision of literal interpretation, enthusiastic secular embrace; describe working-class responses to capitalism (trade unionism as resistance, socialist movement as alternative) and to socialism (enthusiasm among industrial workers, fear among skilled workers, rejection by others); explain what motivated each response — what values, interests or worldviews shaped how different groups received and responded to the same idea; examine how responses shaped what ultimately happened to each idea.
wider: Examine the theological debate within Christianity about evolution — from initial rejection to the accommodation most mainstream churches eventually reached — as a case study in how institutions adapt to challenging ideas

Compare the reception of socialism in Britain (reformist, parliamentary) with Russia (revolutionary) — examining how different social and political conditions produced different responses to the same idea

modes.reason: Students commonly describe responses to ideas as uniformly positive or negative without recognising the diversity of responses within any given group. Multiple examples across different ideas and different responding groups build the nuanced picture the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Investigating a significant individual — role in promoting a key idea
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate the role played by a specific individual in promoting a key idea from the Industrial Revolution period — describing what they did, what idea they promoted, and what they achieved.
criteria: Identifies a specific figure, describes the idea they promoted, and explains at least two things they did to promote it
Evaluates what the figure achieved — whether in their lifetime, through long-term legacy, or in inspiring others

width.minimum: Students select one figure from the period (from: Adam Smith, Florence Nightingale, Pope Leo XIII, William Cuffay, or equivalent), describe what idea they promoted, and explain at least two specific things they did to promote it and what they achieved.
width.typical: Students conduct a structured investigation of one figure: what idea or reform they championed; what their context was (class, occupation, time period, constraints they faced); what strategies they used; what opposition they faced; what they achieved in their lifetime and what legacy they left; evaluate their significance — was their achievement in promoting the idea itself, or in enacting concrete change, or in inspiring others? Examples: Adam Smith systematising free market capitalism through The Wealth of Nations; Florence Nightingale using statistical evidence to reform nursing and hospital sanitation; Pope Leo XIII articulating Catholic social teaching on workers' rights; William Cuffay as a Chartist leader transported to Tasmania.
wider: Investigate a figure not on the standard list — a local figure, a woman, a non-European activist — whose role in promoting industrial-era ideas is less well known but equally important

Evaluate the 'great individual' theory of historical change — to what extent did these individuals shape events, and to what extent did events create the conditions that made these individuals effective?

modes.reason: Students commonly describe historical figures through biographical narrative rather than through an analytical framework. Structuring the investigation around idea-strategies-achievement-evaluation produces a more analytically rigorous account.

descriptors.title: Key features of an Asian society — 18th and early 19th century
descriptors.description: the key social, cultural, economic and political features of an Asian society during the 18th and early 19th Century
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the key features of societies across multiple domains (AC9HH8K07, AC9HH8K12). They have not yet examined Asian societies in the modern period — the political structures, cultural systems, and economic foundations of Qing China, Mughal India, or Tokugawa Japan before European contact became transformative.
elaborations: investigating the significant economic and political features of the Qing dynasty in China
investigating the territorial extent of the Mughal Empire in India
examining the influence of the Tokugawa Shogunate on Japan's political, economic and social development

nodes.label: The Asian society chosen — political structure and authority
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the political structure and basis of authority in their chosen Asian society — explaining who held power, how authority was organised, and what legitimised rule.
nodes.hinge_reason: Political structure is the foundation for understanding social and cultural features (N2) and — critically — for understanding how the society responded to European contact in K20. Students who do not understand the political architecture cannot explain why European contact produced different responses in different Asian societies.
criteria: Describes the political structure of the chosen society with at least two specific features
Explains what legitimised rule in the society's own terms

width.minimum: Students describe the political structure of the chosen society and the basis of its ruler's authority — e.g. the Qing Emperor's Mandate of Heaven, the Mughal Emperor's divine and military authority, the Tokugawa Shogun's feudal control — with at least two specific features.
width.typical: Students describe the full political apparatus — the Emperor/Shogun's role and powers, the administrative hierarchy beneath them, the mechanisms of control (bureaucracy, military, law, ideology); explain what legitimised rule in this society's own terms; describe the stability and instability of the political system; examine the role of specific rulers or political decisions in shaping the society during this period.
wider: Compare the political structure of the chosen Asian society with European political structures of the same period — absolute monarchy, parliamentary systems — identifying similarities and differences
Examine how political authority in the chosen society dealt with internal challenge — rebellion, succession disputes, regional autonomy — to understand the limits of central power

modes.reason: Students commonly describe Asian rulers as powerful without understanding the specific structures and legitimating ideologies — Mandate of Heaven, Shogunal feudalism, Mughal divine kingship — that organised political authority. Making these explicit is the scaffold for the contact-and-change analysis in K20.

nodes.label: Social structure, economy and cultural expression
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the social structure, economic foundations, and significant cultural features of their chosen Asian society.
criteria: Describes the social hierarchy and economic foundations of the chosen society
Describes at least one major cultural feature and explains how it reflected the society's values

width.minimum: Students describe the social hierarchy, the economic basis (trade, agriculture, tribute), and at least one major cultural feature (art, architecture, literature) of the chosen society.
width.typical: Students describe the social hierarchy in their chosen society — the scholar-gentry in Qing China, the caste system under Mughal administration, the rigid samurai-commoner hierarchy of Tokugawa Japan; the economic foundations — tributary systems, agricultural taxation, trade controls; significant cultural features — the Confucian examination system and its cultural role in China, Mughal art and architecture (Taj Mahal, miniature painting), Japanese Noh and Kabuki theatre, samurai aesthetic culture; explain how cultural expression reflected and reinforced political and social values.
wider: Examine a specific cultural artefact from the chosen society — a painting, building, text, or ceremonial object — as a historical source that reveals something about the society's values and worldview

Investigate the role of religion in the chosen society — Confucianism in China, Islam in the Mughal Empire, Buddhism and Shinto in Japan — and how religious institutions shaped social and political life

modes.reason: Students need sufficient encounter with the chosen society's features across multiple domains — political, social, economic, cultural — before they can engage the contact-and-change analysis that K20 requires. Surface familiarity with one feature is insufficient.

descriptors.title: Causes and effects of European contact on an Asian society
descriptors.description: the causes and effects of European contact, including colonialisation, on an Asian society
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the key features of the chosen Asian society (AC9HH9K19) and describe the effects of European imperial expansion (AC9HH9K01). They have not yet examined how European contact specifically transformed the chosen Asian society — what changed, what persisted, and what the society's internal dynamics brought to the encounter.
elaborations: identifying aspects of the Asian society under investigation that remained the same or changed during this period
describing the reasons for and the effects of the British opium trade with China
examining the development of the British Raj and identifying British influences on Indian society
investigating the short- and long-term effects of Dutch trade and colonisation on Indonesian society from the 17th century

nodes.label: Nature and causes of European contact — trade, competition and control
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how European contact with the chosen Asian society developed — from trade to colonisation — and explain the European motivations driving increasing engagement.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how contact developed from trade to control is the prerequisite for understanding both the effects (N2) and continuity/change analysis (N3). Students who see European domination as sudden cannot explain the differential experiences of Asian societies or the varied responses to contact.
criteria: Describes how European contact with the chosen society developed over time
Identifies at least two European motivations for engagement and explains how each drove increasing contact

width.minimum: Students describe how European contact developed over time (from trade to greater control) and identify at least two motivations driving European engagement.
width.typical: Students describe the development of contact — the East India Companies as commercial and then political actors; European competition for trade access (British, Dutch, French, Portuguese); the transformation from commercial relationship to territorial control; explain European motivations — access to goods (spices, silk, tea, opium), strategic positioning, missionary activity, Enlightenment curiosity; describe the specific mechanism of increasing control in the chosen context (opium trade in China, Company rule in India, Dutch VOC in Indonesia).
wider: Examine the opium trade as a case study in how commercial exploitation could be backed by military force — and what this reveals about the relationship between capitalism and imperialism
Compare the mechanisms of European control in two different Asian societies — examining why different societies experienced different types and intensities of European intervention

modes.reason: Students commonly treat European colonisation as a sudden imposition rather than as a gradual process with commercial origins. Making the developmental trajectory explicit — trade → commercial dominance → political control — is the scaffold for understanding how the process unfolded and how it could be resisted at different stages.

nodes.label: Effects of European contact — change and continuity in the chosen society
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify aspects of the chosen Asian society that changed and those that remained the same as a result of European contact.
criteria: Identifies at least two changes resulting from European contact with the chosen society
Identifies at least one significant continuity and explains why it persisted

width.minimum: Students identify at least two changes and at least one continuity in the chosen society resulting from European contact.
width.typical: Students describe changes — political (loss of sovereignty, new legal systems), economic (integration into European trade systems, deindustrialisation, cash crop monocultures), social (new class structures, missionary influence), cultural (spread of European languages, education systems, religion); and continuities — traditional practices, family structures, religious beliefs, cultural arts that persisted under or alongside colonial rule; apply the continuity-change framework from K05; examine how different social groups experienced contact differently — elites who collaborated, peasants who resisted, artisans displaced by imports.
wider: Examine the British Raj's infrastructure legacy (railways, telegraph, schools, law) and evaluate whether its long-term effects were primarily beneficial or harmful — examining the debate from Indian and British perspectives
Investigate how colonial contact changed gender relations in the chosen society — examining what changed for women specifically and what forces drove those changes

modes.reason: Students commonly focus on dramatic political changes (loss of sovereignty) without examining the economic, social and cultural changes that often had greater effects on everyday life. Multiple domains of change — and attention to continuities — build the fuller picture.

descriptors.title: Significant events, ideas and people in the development of an Asian society
descriptors.description: significant events, ideas, people, groups and/or movements in the development of an Asian society
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe how individuals and groups promote ideas and how significant events shape historical change (AC9HH9K18, AC9HH8K05, AC9HH8K10). They have not yet applied this analytical framework to the specific development of the chosen Asian society under European contact pressure.
elaborations: describing the activities of Christian missionaries in China, and the role of the Self-Strengthening Movement and the Society of Righteous Harmony in the Boxer Rebellion
investigating the role of Empress Dowager Cixi in modernising China
examining the role of Emperor Mutsuhito, Commodore Matthew Perry and the Satsuma Rebellion in Japan
describing the role of the British East India Company, the Sepoy Rebellion, the Indian National Congress and key figures in the development of Indian nationalism
examining the contribution of key figures and movements to Indonesian independence

nodes.label: The central tension — tradition vs modernisation under colonial pressure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the central tension facing Asian societies in this period — how to respond to European power while preserving cultural identity — and describe how this tension shaped significant events and movements.
nodes.hinge_reason: The tradition-vs-modernisation tension is the conceptual framework for understanding why specific figures and movements arose. Students who do not understand this tension cannot explain why the Boxer Rebellion and the Self-Strengthening Movement were both responses to the same pressure, or why the Meiji Restoration was so distinctive.
criteria: Explains the tension between modernisation and cultural preservation in the chosen Asian society
Describes how this tension shaped at least one significant event or movement

width.minimum: Students explain that Asian societies faced pressure to modernise (adopt European military and industrial methods) to resist European dominance, while also seeking to preserve their own cultural and political identity, and describe how this tension shaped at least one significant event or movement.
width.typical: Students describe the core dilemma — adopt European methods and risk cultural transformation vs maintain tradition and risk military and economic subordination; examine how this tension produced different responses in different societies (China's Self-Strengthening Movement vs Japanese Meiji modernisation vs Indian nationalism); explain how the tension shaped the movements and figures in the following nodes.
wider: Examine whether this tradition/modernisation tension was unique to Asian societies under European pressure, or whether it reflects a universal pattern in how societies respond to powerful external challenges

modes.reason: Students commonly describe individual events or figures without understanding the common structural tension driving them. Making the modernisation-tradition dilemma explicit is the scaffold for understanding why these specific figures and movements emerged when they did.

nodes.label: Significant events, individuals and movements in the chosen society
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe significant events, individuals, groups and movements in the development of the chosen Asian society, explaining the role each played and what it achieved.
criteria: Describes at least two significant individuals or events in the chosen society's development
Explains the role each played and what it achieved or failed to achieve

width.minimum: Students describe at least two significant individuals or events from the chosen society and explain the role each played in the society's development.
width.typical: For China: the Self-Strengthening Movement, Christian missionaries, Empress Dowager Cixi, the Boxer Rebellion and Society of Righteous Harmony; for Japan: Emperor Mutsuhito (Meiji), Commodore Perry's arrival, the Satsuma Rebellion, samurai resistance to modernisation; for India: the British East India Company, the Sepoy Rebellion, Indian National Congress, Gokhale, Naoroji, Tilak, early Gandhi; for Indonesia: Diponegoro, Java War, Budi Utomo, Sarekat Islam, Sukarno, Hatta, Sjahrir; describe what each figure or movement sought to achieve, what strategies they used, and what they accomplished.
wider: Examine the Boxer Rebellion (or equivalent chosen society event) from both Chinese and European perspectives — analysing how the same events were understood and justified differently
Investigate a figure from the chosen society in depth — examining their motivations, strategies, achievements and legacy

modes.reason: Students commonly focus on the most dramatic or well-known event or figure without building a picture of the range of responses — from accommodation to resistance to modernisation — that characterised the chosen society's development.

descriptors.title: Continuities and changes in an Asian society around the turn of the 20th century
descriptors.description: continuities and changes and their effects on the ways of life and living conditions, political and legal institutions, and cultural expression around the turn of the 20th century in an Asian society
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply the continuity-and-change framework (AC9HH9K05) and describe the effects of European contact (AC9HH9K20). They have not yet applied this framework systematically to their chosen Asian society across multiple domains simultaneously.
elaborations: explaining the position of the Asian society in relation to other nations in the world around the turn of the 20th century, including the influence of significant ideas such as nationalism
describing how increasing foreign influence and imperialism was challenging and changing Asian societies
investigating what remained the same or changed during this period as a result of contact with European powers
comparing the Cultivation System and the Ethical System in the Dutch East Indies (Indonesia)

nodes.label: The chosen society's position in the world around 1900
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the position of the chosen Asian society in relation to other nations around 1900 — including its relationship to European powers, its domestic political situation, and how ideas such as nationalism were influencing it.
nodes.hinge_reason: Establishing the society's position around 1900 is the prerequisite for the continuity-change analysis.
